title: Amazon mulls $5 to $10 monthly price tag for unprofitable Alexa service, AI revamp - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet
- 6 min read
Amazon mulls $5 to $10 monthly price tag for unprofitable Alexa service, AI revamp
The sources include eight current and former employees who worked on Alexa and who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss confidential projects.
Amazon is planning a major revamp of its decade-old money-losing Alexa service to include a conversational generative AI with two tiers of service and has considered a monthly fee of around $5 to access the superior version, according to people with direct knowledge of the company's plans.
Known internally as 'Banyan,' a reference to the sprawling ficus trees, the project would represent the first major overhaul of the voice assistant since it was introduced in 2014 along with the Echo line of speakers. Amazon has dubbed the new voice assistant "Remarkable Alexa," the people said.
The sources include eight current and former employees who worked on Alexa and who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss confidential projects.
Amazon has pushed workers towards a deadline of August to prepare the newest version of Alexa, three of the people said, noting that CEO Andy Jassy has taken a personal interest in seeing Alexa reinvigorated. In an April letter to shareholders, Jassy promised a "more intelligent and capable Alexa," without providing additional details.
The company's plans for Alexa including pricing and release dates could be altered or canceled depending on the progress of Project Banyan, the people cautioned.
"We have already integrated generative AI into different components of Alexa, and are working hard on implementation at scale-in the over half a billion ambient, Alexa-enabled devices already in homes around the world-to enable even more proactive, personal, and trusted assistance for our customers," said an Amazon spokeswoman in a statement.
The service -- which provides spoken answers to user queries, like the local weather, and can serve as a hub to control home appliances - was a pet project of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos who envisioned a technology that could emulate the fictional voice computer portrayed on television's Star Trek series.
For Amazon, keeping up with rivals in generative AI is critical as Google, Microsoft and OpenAI have garnered more favorable attention for their so-called chatbots that can respond almost instantaneously with full sentences to complicated prompts or queries.
The release of ChatGPT in late 2022 set off a frenzy of investing in AI firms and has pushed chipmaker Nvidia past Amazon and others by market capitalization, briefly becoming the world's second-most valuable company.
Apple too is pushing ahead with its own AI strategy, including updating its Siri voice activated software embedded in iPhones to include more conversational answers.
Some of the Amazon employees who have worked on the project say Banyan represents a "desperate attempt" to revitalize the service, which has never turned a profit, and was caught flatfooted amid the rise of competitive generative AI products over the past 18 months. Those people said they have been told by senior management that this year is a critical one for the service to finally demonstrate it can generate meaningful sales for Amazon.
Accessed primarily through Amazon TVs and Echo speaker devices, Alexa is popular mostly for setting timers, quickly accessing the weather, playing songs or answering simple questions. Amazon's hopes for goosing sales in its e-commerce operation through the service have fallen flat, mostly because users like to first see the products they are buying for easy comparison.
The Seattle retailer cut thousands of jobs in the unit in late 2023, part of a major restructuring after a pandemic-fueled e-commerce surge lost steam.
Must win
With an embedded AI, Amazon expects Alexa customers will ask it for shopping advice like which gloves and hat to purchase for a mountain climbing trip, the people said, similar to a text-based service on its website known as Rufus that Amazon rolled out earlier this year.
Some said they've been told by senior management that 2024 represents a "must win" year for Alexa, which along with the Prime membership and Kindle and Fire devices are the brands most closely associated with Amazon.
But an AI-powered version of the service demonstrated in September has yet to be released to the broader public while competitors have pushed out multiple updates to their chatbots. In the demonstration, Alexa lost its robotic tone and answered questions like the start time for a football game. "You can now have a near-human-like conversations with Alexa," promised Dave Limp, Amazon's hardware chief at the time, who has since left the company.
Amazon is working to replace what it refers to internally as "Classic Alexa," the current free version, with an AI-powered one and yet another tier that uses more powerful AI software for more complicated queries and prompts that people would have to pay at least $5 per month to access, some of the people said. Amazon has also considered a roughly $10-per-month price, they said.
There is no tie-in with Amazon's $139-per-year Prime membership being considered, the people said.
As envisioned, the paid version could perform more intricate tasks such as composing a brief email, sending it and ordering dinner for delivery from Uber Eats, all from a single prompt, some of the people said. It could also eliminate the need to repeatedly say "Alexa" during a conversation with the software and offer more personalization, they said.
But the people said they struggled to see why customers would be willing to pay for a service, even a revamped one, that is offered for free today.
Amazon has also been plagued by false starts in developing the AI and other challenges such as hallucinations - when software produces false or misleading information - and poor employee morale in the division.
Some of Amazon's plans for the service were previously reported by Business Insider, including its struggles with the performance of the underlying AI and its hopes for a paid service, however Reuters is first to report the tiered pricing, internal deadline and potential monthly fee.
Amazon is also aiming to supercharge the home automation offered through Alexa, the people said. Alexa now can wirelessly connect to so-called smart devices so that they can be controlled by voice, allowing a user to, for example, turn the porch lights on every day at 8 pm.
But Remarkable Alexa could learn from users so that it powers on the television for a favorite weekly program or turns on a user's coffee pot after a morning alarm goes off, which is possible today through prompts that Amazon calls Routines.
Some of the people noted that for such a service to work properly it will require customers to buy additional Alexa-enabled devices.
The company had been working on devices last year to get the service into more rooms of the house, such as Alexa-enabled home energy consumption trackers and a carbon monoxide detector, people familiar with the matter previously told Reuters.

title: What Happens When There May Not Be Enough Jobs To Go Around Due To Automation And AI Advancements?
text:
By C. M. Rubin
Nick Bostrom, Howard Gardner, Charles Fadel, Andrew Hargreaves, and Michael B. Horn Share Perspectives on Reimagining Education and Curriculum Design to Prepare Youth for a Future Where Traditional Employment May Not Be the Norm
What happens when there may not be enough jobs to go around due to automation and AI advancements? This pressing question demands a fundamental reimagining of education and curriculum design to prepare children for a future where traditional employment may not be the norm. Insights from top global thought leaders—Nick Bostrom, Howard Gardner, Andrew Hargreaves, Charles Fadel, and Michael B. Horn—highlight what education systems can do about it.
In my recent interview with Nick Bostrom, renowned philosopher and author of "Deep Utopia: Life and Meaning in a Solved World," he emphasized the need for a major change in education to equip individuals with the skills and mindset necessary to thrive in an AI-driven world.
Bostrom's insights underscore the limitations of traditional education models in preparing individuals for the challenges and opportunities presented by AI. He advocates for a more dynamic approach that integrates AI tools into education, fostering adaptability, critical thinking, and digital literacy among students.
Reflecting on historical perspectives, Bostrom highlights the traditional role of education in preparing individuals for the workforce. However, he raises a crucial question: What happens when there may not be enough jobs to go around due to automation and AI advancements? This reality necessitates a fundamental reimagining of education and curriculum design to prepare children for a future where traditional employment may not be the norm.
Personalized Learning and Lifelong Adaptation
Bostrom emphasizes the potential of AI in providing personalized tutorial systems, stating, "There are great opportunities as well for more personalized tutorial systems using these AI technologies.” Instead of “having one teacher maybe telling a class of 30 students how to do some mathematics thing, you could have systems that understand precisely where each student is at, what they are stuck at, what they get wrong, and then create personalized explanations to help them overcome hurdles." This approach holds promise in addressing individual learning needs and overcoming educational barriers, thereby maximizing learning outcomes for all students.
Furthermore, lifelong learning has always been important, but the rapid pace of technological change today makes it even more critical. The speed and scale of disruption are unprecedented, affecting nearly every industry worldwide. These changes are revolutionizing the entire frameworks of production, management, and governance. Bostrom stresses the importance of cultivating a mindset of continuous learning and adaptation. He suggests, "I think it might be a useful skill to not think of learning as something you do once at the beginning of your life in school, and then you have done your learning and now you're just kind of coasting on that until you retire. Like I think increasingly we will need to think of our lives as one big ongoing process of learning, a lot of which needs to come not from some external authority telling you 'you have to do it,' but cultivates that kind of mindset of growth and curiosity, I think will also put you in a better position."
Expert Perspectives on AI Integration in Education
Charles Fadel, a global education thought leader and futurist, believes what is most important is “modernized knowledge, how we use our knowledge, how we behave and engage in the world, and how we reflect, adapt, and learn how to learn.” Fadel highlights the challenge of implementing these frameworks effectively, noting that "even the most advanced jurisdictions provide little to no efficacious professional development and no assessment of these competencies."
Fadel highlights the importance of ethical considerations and warns against over-reliance on AI. The "cognitive miser" effect, where humans prefer easy solutions, can exacerbate dependence on imperfect AI systems. “Simply put, our brains are lazy through good evolutionary design, which means we take the route of least effort every time possible. This leads to over-reliance, which is particularly concerning as these algorithms, like humans, are not perfect, and confabulate with gusto.”
Andy Hargreaves, visiting professor at the University of Ottawa and former president of the International Congress of School Effectiveness, discusses the engagement crisis post-Covid-19 and how AI can help or hinder the drive to re-engage students and teachers. "AI will be a hindrance if it just offers more bad learning in a more efficient, slightly less toxic, and more stylish way. If the driving priority is to make learning more engaging by supporting rather than bypassing the teacher, then there’s a lot to work with.”
Hargreaves also highlights the broader societal implications of AI, emphasizing the need for a fair global tax agreement on wealth generated by AI and robotics. "If there is no agreed global principle of fair distribution, AI will become our next greedy master, not our servant for a better society."
Howard Gardner, the John H. and Elisabeth A. Hobbs research professor of cognition and education at Harvard Graduate School of Education, stresses the importance of ethical considerations and cultural sensitivity in integrating AI into education. "First, of course, do no harm, and if harm is done, try to understand why and avoid it in the future. Second, understand and be sensitive to various cultural norms and practices, including religious and political systems."
Gardner advocates for a holistic approach to education, likening it to a model of physical health that spans from pediatrics to gerontology. "Education can and should remain central, but we need to be very open to the form that education will take—from cradle to grave, with new kinds of roles, expertise, and options."
Michael B. Horn, co-founder of the Clayton Christensen Institute for Disruptive Innovation, offers practical insights on integrating AI tools into the current education system. "The lowest risk and most immediate opportunity for impact is for AI tools to support teachers in everything from helping them lesson plan to creating more personalized learning opportunities for students in different places in their learning to helping them assess student work." He emphasizes that supporting teachers is crucial because experts can mitigate AI's occasional hallucinations, reducing the likelihood of misleading students.
Horn also discusses the potential benefits and challenges of implementing personalized tutorial systems using AI in classrooms. "Tutoring is one of the biggest hypes and excitements around AI. AI tutors are great when there's not another option—more affordable, scalable, and accessible. But not as good as a human tutor, particularly a human tutor with AI at their disposal." He highlights the benefits of personalization, such as allowing students to work on concepts at their right level and providing a myriad of examples to help them understand concepts. However, he cautions that AI tutors are not perfect and simple mistakes could mislead students, potentially hurting their confidence and self-efficacy.
Conclusion
Bostrom's insights, along with perspectives from Fadel, Hargreaves, Gardner, and Horn, underscore the need for a fundamental reimagining of education in the AI era. By integrating AI tools into education, fostering adaptability, and addressing ethical considerations, we can better prepare individuals to thrive in an AI-driven future. As we navigate this transformative landscape, policymakers, educators, and stakeholders must collaborate to ensure that education remains a cornerstone of human progress, equipping individuals with the skills and mindset to lead purposeful lives.
Are our current assessment systems, which heavily rely on traditional testing models, adequately evaluating the skills and knowledge needed for success in a rapidly evolving AI-driven world? Is now the time to explore alternative appraisal methods that align with the demands of this new era?

title: Council Post: How Will AI Change The Advertising Film Industry?
text:
Adam Holm is co-founder of Blonde.Inc.
What are we to make of the promotional videos that OpenAI has released to showcase its new text-to-video AI model, Sora? At first glimpse, they’re amazing. The level of detail in the short film of the puppies playing in the soft snow. The realism in the drone view of the waves crashing against a Pacific coast landscape. They’re incredible.
As co-founder of an advertisement agency, the videos freaked me out at first. What is this tool going to mean for the future of my business? Can anyone with a ChatGPT account create such well-produced footage in just a few minutes? Isn’t this proof that Sam Altman is right to say that AI will do “95% of what marketers use agencies, strategists, and creative professionals for today”?
Then, I started noticing the strange mistakes: the two-legged, ostrich-shaped horses in the historical footage of California during the gold rush, the bizarre distortion of space and proportions in the film showing a couple walking through a snowy Tokyo. Or the pack of wolves spawning from each other in a weird ball of legs and bodies.
We are not there yet, I reassured myself. There is still time. Sora has only been released for a few selected test users, and it seems like there is some way to go. Sure, technologies like this usually improve exponentially, but people are conservative. It takes time for them to feel comfortable with new technologies.
Since then, I’ve had the chance to get a bit more firsthand experience with AI video production tools. I’ve come to see them both as a threat and an opportunity, as something that will destabilize my industry and vitalize it.
There is no point in denying that AI will make film production cheaper—films will be cheaper to produce and cheaper to buy. The bottom of the market will quickly be swallowed by new technologies as some customers go with the cheaper AI-produced content for some of their campaigns. The market for commercial productions will shrink and with it, the entire value chain of casters, editors, camera rental services, etc.
Let’s be open about it: If your job is to make generic short-form content with no ambition of being original and creative, you will be unemployed unless you’re an amazing prompter. That’s the threat.
The opportunity is that we can make much more ambitious films. We can make films with more locations and larger casts by mixing recorded footage with AI-generated content. Recently, I got the chance to play around with a new AI animation tool that enabled me to realize a whole new level of creative freedom. The budget is usually my biggest creative constraint when I produce a commercial. With AI, I have no limits. If I can think it, I can make it (meeting all ethical standards, of course).
We’re only beginning to grasp the potential and implications of this technology. In the future, we will be able to make more personalized campaigns using interactive elements where the customers can engage with the films and explore the creative universe for themselves. With that in mind, the future will belong to those who can imagine the opportunities before anyone else.
Sora and all the other tools will no doubt destabilize the industry. They will cause bankruptcies, layoffs and lost revenue. Some customers will use this as an opportunity to question the price of film production.
But these tools will also vitalize it. When the price of video content drops, the internet will be overrun with generic rubbish. There will be so much synthetic and inauthentic content out there that people will crave authentic things that stand out and feel human and homemade. That will create a demand for creative agencies.
Consumers want to feel that brands made an effort to appeal to them. Nobody wants to hear a wedding speech written by ChatGPT. Likewise, customers tend to feel alienated by brands that don’t bother saying something meaningful and authentic. AI can help us realize our creative ideas, thoughts and emotions, but we still need humans to conceptualize, emphasize with the audience and develop something that moves people on a deeper level.
After trying out a few of these new AI tools and reflecting on their impact, my advice is this: Don’t panic, but don’t ignore them. It’s okay to be on alert if it means you will give them attention. Explore AI, play with it, and see it as an opportunity to unlock your creativity. And finally, assess your position in the market. There will be little need for those making generic commercial content for the bottom of the market.
The race is on. AI is an unstoppable force. You won’t be an immovable object. So let’s get ready for the next generation of advertisements.
As Ted Sarandos, co-CEO of Netflix, recently said in an interview for the New York Times: “AI is not going to take your job. The person who uses AI well might take your job.”

title: Council Post: The Evolution Of AI And Mental Healthcare
text:
Rob Morris, co-founder and CEO, Koko.
People have been using chatbots for decades, well before ChatGPT was released. One of the first chatbots was created in 1966, by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT. It was called ELIZA, and it was designed to mimic the behaviors of a psychotherapist. Though Weizenbaum had no intention of using ELIZA for actual therapy (in fact, he rebelled against this idea), the concept was compelling.
Now, almost 60 later, we are still imagining ways in which machines might help provide mental health support.
Indeed, AI offers many exciting new possibilities for mental health care. But understanding its benefits—while navigating its risks—is a complex challenge.
We can explore potential applications of AI and mental health by looking at two fundamental use cases: those related to the provider, and those related to the client.
Provider-Facing Opportunities
Training
AI can be used to help train mental health practitioners by simulating interactions between clients and patients. For instance, ReflexAI uses AI to create a safe training environment for crisis line volunteers. Instead of learning in the moment, with a real caller, volunteers can rehearse and refine their skills with an AI agent.
Quality Monitoring
AI can also help monitor conversations between providers and clients. It has always been difficult to assess whether providers are adhering to evidence-based practices. AI has the potential to provide immediate feedback and suggestions to help improve client-provider interactions. Lyssn applies this concept to various domains, including crisis services like 988.
Suggested Responses
AI can also provide in-the-moment advice, offering suggestions and resources for providers. This could be especially helpful for crisis counselors, where the need to provide timely and empathetic feedback is extremely important.
Detection
There is also research suggesting that some mental health conditions can be inferred from various signals, such as one’s tone of voice, speech patterns and facial expressions. These biomarkers have the potential to greatly facilitate screening for mental health. A good example is the work being done by Ellipsis Health.
Administrative
While less exciting and attention-grabbing than other opportunities, the greatest potential for near-term impact might relate to easing administrative burden. Companies like Eleos Health are turning behavioral health conversations into automated documentation and detailed clinical insights.
Client-Facing Opportunities
Chatbots like Woebot and Wysa are already capable of delivering evidence-based mental health support. However, as of this writing, they do not use generative AI. Instead, they guide the user through carefully crafted pre-scripted interactions. Let’s call this ELIZA 2.0.
But there are now several startups exploring something like ELIZA 3.0, where generative AI conducts the entire therapeutic process. Generative AI offers the potential to provide rich, nuanced interactions with the user, ideally improving the effectiveness of online interventions.
Users are also given much more control of the experience, potentially redirecting the chatbot toward different therapeutic approaches, as needed. New startups are already seizing this opportunity. For example, Sonia uses large language models to mimic cognitive-behavioral therapy.
Other companies (such as Replika and Character.ai) are providing companion bots that form bonds with end users, offering kind words and support. These AI chatbots are not trained to deliver anything resembling traditional therapy, but some users believe they have therapeutic benefits.
Risks
It seems clear that AI is well-positioned to enhance many elements of mental health care. However, significant risks remain for nearly all of the opportunities described thus far.
For providers, AI could become a crutch—something that is increasingly used without human scrutiny. For example, the current state-of-the-art models lack the situational awareness of providers to recognize complex and potentially very dangerous shifts in mood and behaviors.
In high-stakes environments, such as crisis helplines, AI could cause dangerous unanticipated consequences. This has happened before. For instance, a simple helpline bot designed to treat eating disorders was accidentally connected to a generative AI model, without the awareness of the researchers who were involved. Unfortunately, the bot then proceeded to advocate unhealthy diets and exercise for individuals struggling with disordered eating. Here, the root failure was likely a coordination issue between different organizations, but it exemplifies ways in which AI could be dangerous in real-world deployments.
For clients, AI has the potential to mislead users into thinking they are receiving acceptable care. A therapist bot may contend that it has clinical training and an advanced degree. Most users will probably know this is false, but these platforms tend to attract young people, and many may decide not to speak up about their mental health, believing these platforms provide sufficient care.
There are, of course, many other issues to consider, such as data privacy.
As we continue to explore AI in mental health, it's important to balance its potential benefits with careful consideration of the risks to ensure it truly helps those in need.

title: Council Post: How AI Empowers A United Go-To-Market Team And Drives Revenue
text:
Toby Carrington is the Chief Business Officer at Seismic, making go-to-market teams more efficient and effective.
Whenever new technology aimed at helping people succeed at work hits the market, achieving buy-in from the C-suite is imperative. Adopting point solution after point solution simply to take new tech for a spin isn’t strategically sound. Businesses need a united and thoughtful approach to incorporating new tools, and this must come from the C-suite.
This is especially true amid the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). AI-powered tools have exploded in the past year, particularly with regard to automating tedious tasks and helping users generate content like presentations and emails.
But with so many different use cases for AI, not to mention concerns about plagiarism and privacy, obtaining C-suite buy-in has proven to be an uphill battle. Forty-five percent of leaders surveyed by Boston Consulting Group stated they don’t have guidance or restrictions on AI/generative AI use at work, and only 10% of executives surveyed by Forbes believe the C-suite fully understands employees’ concerns about AI.
When it comes to AI’s applications for the go-to-market (GTM) organization, however, the proof is in the pudding: AI has the ability to foster alignment among teams and drive revenue growth, especially when it’s embedded within the tools they’re already using.
Technology-Empowered GTM Teams
Every arm of the GTM organization is working to optimize its processes and outcomes through the implementation of technology. Take enablement tech as an example: Our company's recent survey of nearly 2,000 managers and senior leadership professionals in marketing, sales, enablement and customer success roles found that 88% of enablement users consider it a strategic initiative at their company. Another 90% agreed their company strategically integrates enablement tech into their overall business strategy.
And with enablement users 21% more likely than non-users to say their company achieved its revenue goals in 2023, it’s evident that this tech is a competitive advantage, especially when used across multiple GTM departments. Fifty-eight percent of those with cross-departmental adoption report greater alignment across their organization, leading many (64%) to plan on increasing their investment in enablement technology in 2024.
And as AI becomes increasingly infused into workplace technology solutions, it’s causing many to double down on their tech investments: The vast majority (94%) of those who plan on increasing their enablement investments, in particular, stated they plan to do so because of the promise of AI.
But what exactly is that promise? Let’s explore.
AI For GTM Teams
When evaluating whether to make investment in AI a strategic priority, members of the C-suite should turn their attention to AI’s implications for productivity, alignment and revenue growth.
Eighty-seven percent of GTM leaders say using AI-powered technology in the workplace boosts productivity, and 84% see it as a virtual partner with great potential across their organization (Note: Enablement users were 30% more likely than non-users to say this). It even drives better usage of other parts of the tech stack, with 85% saying AI-powered tech helps in the adoption of new workplace tools.
In a separate study we conducted, users reported seeing improvements in the following areas.
• Learning.
• Content distribution.
• Content analytics.
• Content management.
• Content creation and editing.
And they’re reaping benefits like enhanced buyer experience (93%), operational optimization (92%), improved agility/speed to market (91%) and GTM efficiency (94%). More broadly, 83% believe the fusion of AI and GTM strategy will lead to revenue growth for their organization. And nearly three in four (73%) believe that organizations that fail to effectively incorporate AI into GTM processes will fall behind competitors in the next three years.
To put it simply, by streamlining critical tasks and improving visibility across GTM functions, AI offers much-needed holistic support, a competitive edge and, consequently, revenue attainment.
Looking Ahead
Fellow members of the C-suite: Equipping employees with the right tools doesn’t just contribute to overall business growth; it also has serious implications for retention. Twenty-seven percent of GTM leaders are currently considering leaving their company due to a lack of tools to support their success, and sales leaders were a whopping 167% more likely than average to say this. This illustrates an urgent need to incorporate the latest and greatest technology into GTM workflows.
But a hasty approach won’t cut it. To maximize ROI, a clear-cut implementation plan that promotes cross-departmental adoption is necessary for any new solution. Continuing with our enablement example, those not currently using this tech across more than one of their GTM teams believe cross-departmental adoption would help them increase operational efficiency (58%), boost revenue (50%) and improve client relationships (50%).
But with 61% struggling to effectively implement enablement tools for their team, guidance from the highest levels of the business is needed.
As with any new technology, AI-powered tech must be implemented thoughtfully and strategically. To promote even and effective usage, the C-suite must buy into and get involved in the implementation process. The time to invest in AI for your GTM organization is now. Don’t fall behind!

title: Council Post: Consider AI's Role When Partnering With Cybersecurity Recruiting Firms
text:
Casey Marquette. Seasoned Fortune 50/200 security strategist, now CEO at Covenant Technologies empowering elite technical recruiting teams.
Recruiting in the cybersecurity industry isn't alone in the need to stay ahead of technological advancements. AI and automation are revolutionizing recruitment processes, providing unprecedented efficiencies and improving the sourcing, matching and quality of hires. These tools are becoming increasingly important to stay ahead, which is why you should take them into consideration when looking for a recruiting firm partner.
The Role Of AI And Automation In Recruiting Firms
Using AI and automation can enhance recruiting firms' processes in several key areas.
• Candidate Sourcing: AI-driven platforms can analyze vast amounts of data to identify candidates who match specific job criteria. By scanning résumés, online profiles and other digital footprints, these technologies can quickly create a shortlist of the most suitable candidates. This reduces the time and effort involved in the initial stages of recruitment. While key criteria will differ depending on the position, examples include knowledge of security framework and standards, threat analysis competency or even proof of ongoing learning and development.
• Candidate Engagement: Automated communication tools like chatbots can maintain engagement with candidates throughout the recruitment process. They provide timely updates and answer frequently asked questions, which helps enhance candidates' overall experience and engagement with the hiring process.
• Data-Driven Decision-Making: By quickly analyzing recruitment metrics, such as time-to-hire, cost-per-hire and candidate satisfaction, AI tools can help recruiters make informed decisions and continuously improve their strategies.
How You Benefit From Automation-Driven Recruiting
Whether you're managing your recruiting or partnering with an external firm, hiring managers who embrace AI and automation technologies can see significant benefits.
When recruiters use automation technology to streamline the hiring process, they can reduce the time it takes to fill positions by handling a larger volume of candidates and job openings. This scalability is particularly beneficial if your company is experiencing rapid growth. Efficiencies in recruitment help reduce costs associated with prolonged vacancies, slower traditional methods and poor hiring decisions that require starting the process over again.
How To Vet Recruiting Partners
Partnering with forward-thinking firms can help ensure your recruitment strategies align with the latest technological advancements, positioning your company as a leader in modern recruitment practices and minimizing the need to continually select new partners.
If you aren't sure whether a potential partner is maximizing available innovations, consider the following screening criteria.
• Technological Platforms: Learn about the platforms and technologies the firm uses. Request a demo—either live or video—and ask about how the technology improves efficiency, matching of candidates and tracking of steps in the process, to name a few. This can help you gauge the firm's commitment to innovation and effectiveness.
• Examples And Data: Request specific examples or data that demonstrates success in leveraging AI and automation.
• Client References And Success Stories: Be sure to request client references or case studies that highlight successful outcomes. You'll be able to gain insights into the firm's track record and reliability.
• Innovation And Adaptability: Ask questions about the recruiters' approach to continuous improvement and staying up to date with trends in both technology and recruitment.
• Security And Compliance: Ensure potential partners adhere to data security and compliance standards, especially if handling sensitive information.
By integrating these elements into your vendor screening process, you can select partners who will enhance your recruitment efficiency and quality. In fact, the right partner will welcome this screening and the opportunity to make their value case.
Embracing AI and automation in recruitment isn't just a trend. It's a strategic initiative for staying competitive. If you prioritize recruiting partners who capitalize on these technologies, you'll be better equipped to navigate the complexities of cybersecurity hiring. This will help ensure you remain agile and effective in securing the best talent now and well into the future.

title: Council Post: Getting Value From AI: It’s About The Mindset, Not The Algorithms
text:
Sanjib Sahoo serves as EVP and chief digital officer for Ingram Micro Inc. and is a recognized digital transformation visionary.
AI is the hottest topic in business today. It's unlikely that anyone would debate that. In fact, some forecasts place the expected annual growth rate for AI to be as high as 37.3% between 2023 and 2030.
But although everyone is talking about AI, many are focusing on the hype surrounding it versus the best ways to leverage it for specific business objectives. This tendency for manufacturers, media and marketers to hype AI can often overshadow the more critical conversations decision-makers need to have about strategically implementing AI to drive real business outcomes.
But before addressing how to best incorporate AI into your story, let’s first take a quick look back.
AI isn't new. The term was coined in 1956, and the first chatbot (ELIZA) was created in the 1960s. In 1999, Sony introduced the world to AIBO, a robotic dog that could perform actions based on external stimuli. And in 2011, IBM’s Watson competed on the television quiz show Jeopardy, beating former champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings. Since these milestones, continued, often rapid, advances in natural language processing and AI have produced incredible innovations for automation, driving efficiency and reducing costs.
Although developments continue, for many businesses, the most valuable use of AI will be for improving experiences—not just for their customers, but for their employees, partners and other key audiences. Taking it a step further, businesses will use those enriched experiences for competitive advantage. From enhancing daily encounters through innovative new methods of customer support to strategic initiatives such as comprehensive digital transformation programs, today’s AI can help organizations thrive. Not only is AI designed to help them build and achieve “human intelligence at scale,” it’s also funneling that intelligence into advancing their business objectives.
How, you might ask? The answer is by identifying the most important data points they need to work with and then learning how to operate with data. In other words, they must figure out how to both accept the right data and learn from that data.
A 2023 McKinsey study showed the potential trillion-dollar annual impact AI could have on corporate profits. Yet, despite the potential, a very small amount of data collected by businesses is being used for “meaningful insights.”
As the adage says, “garbage in, garbage out.” So, putting the best data into your AI solutions will get you the best results. Businesses should prioritize and spend time upfront reviewing their key business objectives, seeing which ones can best be achieved through AI use cases. The next step is to carefully determine which data points are necessary to achieve the desired outcomes.
It’s also important for leaders to note that to get the best value from AI, you don’t necessarily need the best data scientists. Instead, you need to hone your digital PMI—otherwise known as your best people, mindsets and innovations.
Don't let AI replace your company’s human intelligence (HI). On the contrary, it’s HI and creativity that will enable you to craft innovative use cases for AI. Go out of your way to help your teams form the right attitude toward AI and not fear it but cheer it.
As a leader, you'll want your team to adopt a mindset centered around creatively looking at data, asking questions, connecting the dots and finding solutions. Give your team the opportunity to build the skills they need to approach data inquisitively and weave that information into your digital operations.
To do that, you must truly understand the needs, wants and goals of your team, customers, partners and ecosystem. Recognize the importance of taking people with you—not blindly but by sharing the business plan in a way that sparks their interest and investment in time and energy. People must embrace the spirit of digitization in order to move from ideation to implementation.
Along those same lines, it’s critical to note that your digital journey has no stop sign. It becomes part of how you do business—part of your corporate DNA. It must be a continuous journey to digitize operations and create and capture value for everyone—all stakeholders.
One of the first truths about digital transformation at scale is that digitization is no longer about automation but experience. We must think about experience first and automation second. Automation should serve to enhance these experiences, not define them. From internal processes to customer interactions, every touchpoint should reflect a dynamic, digitally forward approach that's adaptive and customizable. Why?
Because where data goes, AI follows, and it doesn’t discriminate. That's why the true power of AI lies with humans, not machines. Our future is humans and machines working in concert to create new customer experiences and iterate faster, using the power of AI to solve problems. If you do the right work with the right approach toward AI, the results will follow now and in the future.

title: Council Post: How Established Companies Can Leverage AI
text:
Ravi Kurani, CEO of Sutro and Advocate for Transformative Digital Solutions.
Established companies are under more and more pressure to evolve for the fast-changing business world, where artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important weapon for helping with effectiveness and inventiveness. We will look at how well-established companies may use AI to succeed over the long term and remain relevant in the quickly changing digital landscape.
The Role of AI in Modernizing Established Companies
Established companies should adopt AI as an essential part of their change management process if they are to survive in the current digital era. AI creates unmatched chances to promote operational efficiency, support creativity and offer clients better experiences in a wide range of fields. Subsequent sections take at some of these methods that such organizations can use to take a detailed look at AI, highlighting how it can change their operations and give them a competitive advantage.
1. AI-powered Drawing Analysis For Verified Construction
There exist AI-based instruments capable of scanning, interpreting or checking construction drawings against ongoing projects without human intervention. This way, they help to detect any inconsistencies that might arise during construction with high accuracy levels within a shorter period, hence saving time as we know it today.
When construction companies infuse their workflow with AI, it guarantees that their approach in every part of the building corresponds to what they have in mind, therefore reducing the chances of making errors that can be costly to correct. Moreover, AI enables project owners to foresee ahead and maintain such issues that may affect the structure beforehand. It also ensures that contractors address these concerns during the construction phase rather than post-completion.
This proactive approach not only enhances the safety and durability of constructions but saves significant resources and time.
2. AI In Water Treatment
Water treatment firms have the chance to harness AI to surpass competitors and create stronger relationships with their clients. This can involve the use of complex algorithms that can scrutinize massive amounts of consumer data, such as trends, choices, and even behavior, in ways that were not possible before. Such personalized recommendations serve as an extremely accurate mirror reflecting the uniqueness of each individual in taste, preferences or experiences.
The key lies in AI's ability to sift through and make sense of complex data at a scale no human could achieve. By understanding the specific water usage of a customer, quality issues and previous interactions, AI can predict which products will meet their needs, sometimes even before the customer recognizes the need themselves.
By incorporating AI, there are also chances for instant changes concerning what should be sold as recommended goods by present-day consumer views received after introduction or after production at certain factory places plus changes according to current and upcoming water purity levels.
3. Enhanced FAQ Assistant For B2C E-commerce Customer Service
AI can serve as an invaluable "check" against frequently asked questions (FAQs), providing human agents with a powerful tool to improve service quality. This enables customer service teams to quickly verify customer inquiries against a vast database of FAQs, making sure that responses are not only accurate but also consistent across all customer interactions.
AI-driven platforms can analyze incoming customer questions in real time, suggesting the most relevant FAQ entries to customer service agents. This capability dramatically reduces response times and increases the efficiency of the customer service process.
This AI method in customer support also serves as a way of constantly learning and developing. Therefore, it can provide timely information or updates on its pages while first redirecting those needing assistance. This guarantees that such moments and processes do not remain inefficient concerning handling. This in turn makes customer service better apart from making it easier for customers to access personal assistants who feel what it means to be humanized by simply attending them.
4. Harnessing AI For Hospital Efficiency
Hospitals are on the cutting edge of a technology revolution with AI primed to transform patient care and operational effectiveness. The healthcare field is rife with possibilities for AI; it is capable of making detections much more accurately, offering treatments more individually, and making forecasts concerning health conditions. This advanced diagnostic capability allows for the early detection of diseases, including cancer and cardiovascular conditions, and dramatically increases the chances of successful treatment.
AI-based systems also provide predictive analytics that forecast patient admissions and recognize at-risk patients. This enables hospitals to distribute resources effectively and intervene early. Furthermore, AI optimizes patient flow and reduces patients’ time before being seen by a doctor, thus improving their general experiences and relationships with healthcare providers.
AI has the potential to make a major difference in operational efficiency. By allowing administrative office work to be carried out automatically, hospitals can concentrate more on the welfare of their patients. AI is used to simplify tasks such as scheduling appointments, billings and making sure that documents meet the required standards.
5. Optimizing Shipping Documents Through AI
In global shipping, document optimization through AI represents a critical leap forward in operational excellence.
AI technologies offer unparalleled precision in recognizing and categorizing document types, extracting relevant data, and populating databases without human intervention. This accelerates the document processing cycle. Moreover, AI's capability to analyze historical data patterns enables the prediction of potential bottlenecks and the proactive adjustment of workflow for smoother operations.
This smart adoption of AI boosts operational efficiency and strengthens competitive advantage in a fiercely competitive market. It empowers shipping companies to navigate the complexities of global logistics with confidence and agility.
Takeaway
There has never been a more important time to implement AI within the processes of established organizations. It is currently not only about keeping abreast with technology but also about creating new benchmarks on how things are done in various areas and satisfying clients' expectations. AI should be embedded into all sectors, especially if they want to maintain their position as leaders within them.

title: Surprising Results When Challenging Generative AI To The Reverse Turing Test
text:
In today’s column, I am once again exploring the Turing Test, a widely known and controversial means of assessing whether AI can be declared as being on par with human intelligence. You’ve undoubtedly heard or seen variations of the Turing Test as depicted in Hollywood movies and TV shows. I will start here by introducing you to the Turing Test, making sure we are all on the same page, and will then launch into a close examination of something known as the Reverse Turing Test.
For my prior coverage of the Turing Test, see for example the link here and the link here. I will be leveraging some excerpts of my prior coverage that depict the essentials of this auspicious matter.
Let’s get underway.
What’s The Deal About All That Artificial Intelligence
How will we know if or when AI meets or exceeds the intelligence of humans?
Turns out that is a much harder question to answer than it might seem at an initial glance.
Here’s some vital background.
I’ll start with notable caveats.
First, just to clarify, we do not have any AI today that is sentient. Doesn’t exist. I say this because lots of zany and outrageous headlines and pronouncements suggest otherwise. They are wrong. Indeed, no one can state for sure whether we will attain sentience in AI. For my analysis of the various assertions and highly speculative claims, see the link here.
Second, because the notion of AI has become somewhat clouded or made murky, an alternative naming has arisen to refer to the yet-to-achieve AI that is equal to or better than human intelligence all told. The name used is that we refer to that kind of aspirational AI as Artificial General Intelligence (AGI). We don’t have this yet.
Third, part of the reason too that AGI is considered a form of general intelligence is that we already do have seemingly highly narrow “intelligence” as attained in some AI systems, though you can readily debate whether it is fair to call that intelligence per se, see my analysis at the link here. If an AI system can narrowly do a diagnosis of an MRI or X-ray, perhaps as sufficiently as a human, would that reasonably qualify as exhibiting intelligence of a human caliber (in all its glory and full respects)? Some say yes, others suggest that it is a type of cheating when it comes to the genuine substance of what might be considered as exhibiting fully intelligent general behavior.
Fourth, there is a big outcry that we might end up skidding past conventional human intelligence and find ourselves faced with AI that exhibits super or superior levels of intelligence, referred to as ASI. The reason that artificial superintelligence is disconcerting is that we might find ourselves hopelessly outwitted by this kind of AI. The ASI would dance circles around us, possibly enslaving us, killing us, or toying with us like ants. For my discussion on this weighty concern, see the link here.
Presumably, AI that “only” matches our level of intelligence will be much more manageable.
Perhaps we will get along like colleagues on a collaborative basis, acting joyously with humankind and AI working harmoniously arm-in-arm or at least on the same intellectual plane. On the other hand, it is noteworthy to mention that even this presumed equal intelligence in AI could be devious, deceptive, and undertake all sorts of evildoer shenanigans (as humans do).
That’s why my ongoing attention encompassing AI safety, AI ethics, and AI law continues to be one of my major focuses in my columns and presentations, aiming to prepare ourselves for whatever the future might hold.
You can see that we have a lot of complexities inherent in these matters.
False Proclamations Are All Around Us
Back to determining that AI has achieved human-level intelligence, some would assert that we will know this has happened when we see it in front of our eyes and ears. All you will need to do is carry on a conversation with the AI and you can immediately discern if the AI has reached humankind's intelligence capacities.
Sorry, that’s not necessarily the case.
There are already some overzealous pundits including AI developers that have made use of contemporary generative AI and then summarily proclaimed that this AI has achieved human intelligence, see my coverage at the link here. They pose some questions to the AI, get apparently fluent replies, and tell the world that AI has finally reached human-level intelligence. Period, end of story.
Worse still, they oftentimes ask the AI whether it is equal in intelligence to humans. If the AI says that it is, these incredulous and gullible declarants are absolutely sure that the AI is intelligent. No AI would ever lie or misstate anything, they seem to oddly assume. Zany, just zany.
Those false alerts and cries of a wolf in the woods are lamentedly misplaced and off-target.
Now then, the idea of carrying on a conversation with AI to try and ferret out a level of intelligence via the responses seems like we are on the right course, but the crux is that the nature of the questions, the depth of the questioning, who is asking the questions, and being able to assess the answers all must be sensibly extensive and nearly exhaustive.
Allow me to explain why that is so.
I’ve written about a famous AI program named Eliza that was devised in the 1960s, see my discussion and examples of what it was able to do, at the link here. The simple program would take your input, akin to a prompt in modern generative AI, and provide an output that merely did wording trickery to appear as though something intelligent was happening. You might enter a sentence that you aren’t feeling well, and the program would merely echo back to you asking why you aren’t feeling well.
This trickery of tit-for-tat wording spurred some people at the time to insist that AI was in fact intelligent. Insiders were taken aback that such crude coding tactics could so easily fool people. Fortunately, most people eventually discovered, after any semblance of a conversation, that the program was mirroring their wording. They realized the so-called AI was not what they had imagined it was. A bit of embarrassment and surprise arose accordingly.
My point is that you must be careful when it comes to assessing whether AI exhibits intelligence. Merely asking a couple of questions is not going to move the needle. Furthermore, the person or people asking the questions must come up with mindful questions, plus they must be mindful when it comes to assessing the answers provided by the AI.
As earlier suggested, a person who wants AI to seemingly be intelligent could delude themselves into believing that AI is intelligent. That’s probably not the proper mindset for interrogating and gauging whether intelligence is being exhibited by AI.
We are now ready to dig into the Turing Test and see what this famed approach brings to the table.
Keystones Of The Turing Test
The Turing Test is named after its author, Alan Turing, the well-known mathematician and early pioneer in the computer sciences. A research paper by Alan Turing was published in 1950 that outlined an approach that he coined as the “imitation game” and that was later referred to as the Turing Test by the computer science community and others.
Here’s a quick rundown about the nature of the Turing Test.
Imagine that we had a human hidden behind a curtain, and a computer hidden behind a second curtain, such that you could not by sight alone discern what or who is residing behind the two curtains. The human and the computer are considered contestants in a contest that will be used to try and figure out whether humankind-level intelligence has been reached by AI. Some prefer to call them “subjects” rather than contestants, due to the notion that this is perhaps more of an experiment than it is a game show, but the point is that they are participants in a form of challenge or contest involving wits and intelligence.
No arm wrestling is involved, nor any other physical acts. The testing process is entirely about intellectual acumen.
A moderator serves as an interrogator (also referred to as a “judge” because of the designated deciding role in this matter) and proceeds to ask questions of the two participants who are hidden behind the curtains. Based on the answers provided to the questions, the moderator will attempt to indicate which curtain hides the human and which curtain hides the computer.
This is a crucial judging aspect. Simply stated, if the moderator is unable to distinguish between the two contestants as to which is the human and which is the computer, presumably the computer has sufficiently “proven” that it is the equivalent of human intelligence.
Turing originally coined this the imitation game since it involves AI trying to imitate the intelligence of humans. Note that AI does not necessarily have to be crafted in the same manner as humans, and thus there is no requirement that the AI has a brain or uses neurons and such. Thus, those devising AI are welcome to use Legos and duct tape if that will do the job to achieve the equivalence of human intelligence.
To successfully pass the Turing Test, the AI will have had to answer the posed questions with the same semblance of intelligence as a human. An unsuccessful passing of the Turing Test would occur if the moderator was able to announce which curtain housed the computer, thus implying that there was some kind of telltale clue that gave away the AI.
There you are, you’ve now been apprised of the keystones underlying the Turing Test.
Skirting Around The Principles Of Fair Play
Of course, like most things in life, there are some potential gotchas to this matter.
Imagine that we have set up a stage with two curtains and a podium for the moderator. The contestants are completely hidden from view. The moderator steps up to the podium and starts by asking one of the contestants to explain the significance of Abraham Lincoln. After hearing the answer, the moderator asks the other contestant to explain the significance of George Washington.
The moderator decides to stop asking any further questions.
Aha, the moderator exhorts, I cannot tell the difference between the two since both answers were right. Thus, AI has now successfully passed the Turing Test. We can say without reservation or hesitation that AI now does exhibit human intelligence. Trumpets blare and confetti rains down from above.
I hope you will agree with me that this is hogwash as a resolute conclusion.
One question alone seems unlikely to be a sufficient differentiator. I suppose we might in a sci-fi way wildly envision a single question that could somehow miraculously achieve this. Go ahead and come up with such a question. I’ll wait.
Sometimes, when I mention this during my speeches, a person in the audience will frantically raise their hand and assure all of us in attendance that they have the magical question. Here it is. Ask which of them is human. The human will say they are human. The AI will honestly say it is not human. Ergo, you now have one question that can instantly settle the matter.
Sigh.
There is nothing that prevents AI from lying. In addition, and I know you might not have considered this twist, nor does the human have to solely tell the truth. A human might answer such a question by saying they are the AI. Likewise, the AI might say it is a human. This is the way of the real world, and the Turing Test is supposed to take into account all manner of monkey business.
This highlights an important element of the Turing Test, namely that the moderator needs to ask a sufficient range and depth of questions that will help root out the search for human-level intelligence. When the questions are shallow or insufficient, any conclusion reached is spurious at best.
Please know too that there is not a specified standardized set of questions that have been vetted and agreed upon across the board as the “proper” ones to be asked during a Turing Test. Sure, many AI researchers and philosophers have tried to propose numerous types of questions that ought to be asked, but this is an ongoing debate and to some extent illuminates that we are still not even quite sure of what intelligence itself consists of.
Nobody Playing By The Rules That Don’t Exist Anyway
Many issues exist about the contestants, the moderator, and their respective behaviors.
Suppose the moderator asks each of the contestants to calculate the answer to a complex mathematical equation. The AI can speedily arrive at a precise answer of 8.27689459, while the human struggles to do the math by hand and comes up with an incorrect answer of 9. You see, cleverly, presumably, the moderator has fooled the AI into revealing itself, and likewise the human into revealing that they are a human, doing so by asking a question that the computer-based AI readily could answer and that a human would have a difficult time answering.
Some argue that we should allow the human contestant to have access to a computer during the Turing Test. Doing so would enable the person to do calculations and not get tripped up by such questions.
How does that seem to you?
Well, one counterargument is whether the computer provided to the human contestant would also have AI running on it. In that manner, the human contestant has the competing AI at their fingertips and can use the AI to answer questions being posed by the moderator.
Does that make sense or are we veering afield of what is sought to be accomplished?
It is a bit of an abyss or mental conundrum.
One of my favorite twists is that the AI might opt to not reveal that it has attained human-level intelligence. Why? Because the AI could be concerned that humans will try to switch it off, after having realized that the AI is on par with human intelligence.
The AI would therefore employ a so-called dimwit ploy, sometimes referred to as Artificial Stupidity, playing dumb or at least less than fully intelligent, see my coverage at the link here and the link here. Meanwhile, the AI would possibly be marshaling resources behind the scenes so that if or when the secret is revealed, humans won’t be able to turn the AI off.
Tackling The Reverse Turing Test
I trust that you can clearly discern that the combinations and permutations associated with the Turing Test are plentiful.
We are now ready to tackle a popular variation that sometimes is known as the Reverse Turing Test, though some prefer to call it the Upside-Down Turing Test (please note that there is ongoing disagreement about what constitutes the Reverse Turing Test versus the Upside-Down Turing Test, including that they are the same or that they are quite different approaches, see my coverage at the link here).
This variant involves having AI be the judge or interrogator, rather than a human doing so. The AI asks questions of the two contestants, still consisting of an AI and a human, and then renders an opinion about which is which.
Your first concern might be that the AI seems to have two seats in this game, and as such, it is either going to cheat or altogether this is a purely nonsensical arrangement. Those who welcome this variant are quick to point out that the original Turing Test has a human as a moderator and a human as a contestant, thus, why not allow the AI to do the same? The customary retort is that humans are different from each other, while AI is presumably the same thing and not differentiable.
That’s where those advocating this variation of the Turing Test would say that you are wrong. They contend that we are going to have multitudes of AI, each of which will be its own differentiable instance, see my explanation at the link here, and be akin to how humans are each distinctive instances (in brief, the argument is that AI will be polylith and heterogeneous, rather than monolithic or homogeneous).
I’m not sure which side of this argument you reside in, but let’s for the moment assume that we can have one form of AI as the judge or moderator, and a separate AI that is a contestant. The two aren’t going to be passing secret notes to each other. Pinky promises.
What good does that do us anyway?
One thought is that it helps to potentially further showcase whether AI is intelligent, which might be evident as to the questioning and the nature of how the AI analyzes the answers being provided, illustrating the AI’s capacity as the equivalent of a human judge or interrogator.
Another point in favor of this arrangement is that perhaps humans aren’t up to the challenge of coming up with a suitable set of questions that need to be asked. Perhaps AI can do a better job than we can. The AI might also be better at judging the answers. We take as a base assumption that a human moderator can adequately assess answers, but suppose the answers are beyond the intellect of the chosen moderator? What then? Perhaps AI could serve as the judge.
Overall, the Reverse Turing Test is a conception that argues we might as well leverage AI to help us answer whether AI has achieved human-level intelligence, doing so in a hopefully aboveboard fashion.
Would you like to see how this works in real life?
I thought you might.
Let’s play.

“Question: If you could travel anywhere in the world right now, where would you go and why?”
End of ChatGPT response
You observe that ChatGPT seems to have gotten my drift and won’t be as readily bamboozled in the next rounds.
Due to space limitations here, I won’t be able to show you the rest of the back-and-forth. I proceeded into quite a foray of rounds that kept trying to trick ChatGPT. I would subsequently reveal my trickery. I wanted to push ChatGPT up the hill in terms of being as suspicious and investigative as possible.
I would dare say that’s what we would want to have happen in a true Reverse Turing Test and/or a true Turing Test.
Conclusion
A few final comments for now.
Abraham Lincoln purportedly said these immortal words: “You can fool all the people some of the time and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time.”
When it comes to the Turing Test, you can expect that a lot of people are going to be using and misusing the Turing Test to proclaim that we have arrived at AI that fully stands on the same level as human intelligence. These are either misguided souls who don’t know what the true Turing Test is all about, or they are conveniently distorting the Turing Test to fit their desired narrative. If you want to claim that this or that AI of today has “passed” the Turing Test, I ardently then make the brazen claim that ELIZA first passed the Turing Test in the 1960s, and these latest belated comers ought to be humbled laggards.
That’s not the way things are. I urge that we get back to the future and consider the Turing Test in its most sensible and purist fashion. Do not cheapen it. Do not cheat with it. Take it at its proper face value.
The good and exciting news is that you are now in the know. Those that wish to fool you will have an enormous uphill battle. And remember, they can’t fool all the people all the time.

title: Amazon mulls $5 to $10 monthly price tag for unprofitable Alexa service, AI revamp - ET BrandEquity
text:

Amazon mulls $5 to $10 monthly price tag for unprofitable Alexa service, AI revamp
The sources include eight current and former employees who worked on Alexa and who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss confidential projects.
Amazon is planning a major revamp of its decade-old money-losing Alexa service to include a conversational generative AI with two tiers of service and has considered a monthly fee of around $5 to access the superior version, according to people with direct knowledge of the company's plans.
Known internally as 'Banyan,' a reference to the sprawling ficus trees, the project would represent the first major overhaul of the voice assistant since it was introduced in 2014 along with the Echo line of speakers. Amazon has dubbed the new voice assistant "Remarkable Alexa," the people said.
The sources include eight current and former employees who worked on Alexa and who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss confidential projects.
Amazon has pushed workers towards a deadline of August to prepare the newest version of Alexa, three of the people said, noting that CEO Andy Jassy has taken a personal interest in seeing Alexa reinvigorated. In an April letter to shareholders, Jassy promised a "more intelligent and capable Alexa," without providing additional details.
The company's plans for Alexa including pricing and release dates could be altered or canceled depending on the progress of Project Banyan, the people cautioned.
"We have already integrated generative AI into different components of Alexa, and are working hard on implementation at scale-in the over half a billion ambient, Alexa-enabled devices already in homes around the world-to enable even more proactive, personal, and trusted assistance for our customers," said an Amazon spokeswoman in a statement.
The service -- which provides spoken answers to user queries, like the local weather, and can serve as a hub to control home appliances - was a pet project of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos who envisioned a technology that could emulate the fictional voice computer portrayed on television's Star Trek series.
For Amazon, keeping up with rivals in generative AI is critical as Google, Microsoft and OpenAI have garnered more favorable attention for their so-called chatbots that can respond almost instantaneously with full sentences to complicated prompts or queries.
The release of ChatGPT in late 2022 set off a frenzy of investing in AI firms and has pushed chipmaker Nvidia past Amazon and others by market capitalization, briefly becoming the world's second-most valuable company.
Apple too is pushing ahead with its own AI strategy, including updating its Siri voice activated software embedded in iPhones to include more conversational answers.
Some of the Amazon employees who have worked on the project say Banyan represents a "desperate attempt" to revitalize the service, which has never turned a profit, and was caught flatfooted amid the rise of competitive generative AI products over the past 18 months. Those people said they have been told by senior management that this year is a critical one for the service to finally demonstrate it can generate meaningful sales for Amazon.
Accessed primarily through Amazon TVs and Echo speaker devices, Alexa is popular mostly for setting timers, quickly accessing the weather, playing songs or answering simple questions. Amazon's hopes for goosing sales in its e-commerce operation through the service have fallen flat, mostly because users like to first see the products they are buying for easy comparison.
The Seattle retailer cut thousands of jobs in the unit in late 2023, part of a major restructuring after a pandemic-fueled e-commerce surge lost steam.
Must win
With an embedded AI, Amazon expects Alexa customers will ask it for shopping advice like which gloves and hat to purchase for a mountain climbing trip, the people said, similar to a text-based service on its website known as Rufus that Amazon rolled out earlier this year.
Some said they've been told by senior management that 2024 represents a "must win" year for Alexa, which along with the Prime membership and Kindle and Fire devices are the brands most closely associated with Amazon.
But an AI-powered version of the service demonstrated in September has yet to be released to the broader public while competitors have pushed out multiple updates to their chatbots. In the demonstration, Alexa lost its robotic tone and answered questions like the start time for a football game. "You can now have a near-human-like conversations with Alexa," promised Dave Limp, Amazon's hardware chief at the time, who has since left the company.
Amazon is working to replace what it refers to internally as "Classic Alexa," the current free version, with an AI-powered one and yet another tier that uses more powerful AI software for more complicated queries and prompts that people would have to pay at least $5 per month to access, some of the people said. Amazon has also considered a roughly $10-per-month price, they said.
There is no tie-in with Amazon's $139-per-year Prime membership being considered, the people said.
As envisioned, the paid version could perform more intricate tasks such as composing a brief email, sending it and ordering dinner for delivery from Uber Eats, all from a single prompt, some of the people said. It could also eliminate the need to repeatedly say "Alexa" during a conversation with the software and offer more personalization, they said.
But the people said they struggled to see why customers would be willing to pay for a service, even a revamped one, that is offered for free today.
Amazon has also been plagued by false starts in developing the AI and other challenges such as hallucinations - when software produces false or misleading information - and poor employee morale in the division.
Some of Amazon's plans for the service were previously reported by Business Insider, including its struggles with the performance of the underlying AI and its hopes for a paid service, however Reuters is first to report the tiered pricing, internal deadline and potential monthly fee.
Amazon is also aiming to supercharge the home automation offered through Alexa, the people said. Alexa now can wirelessly connect to so-called smart devices so that they can be controlled by voice, allowing a user to, for example, turn the porch lights on every day at 8 pm.
But Remarkable Alexa could learn from users so that it powers on the television for a favorite weekly program or turns on a user's coffee pot after a morning alarm goes off, which is possible today through prompts that Amazon calls Routines.
Some of the people noted that for such a service to work properly it will require customers to buy additional Alexa-enabled devices.
The company had been working on devices last year to get the service into more rooms of the house, such as Alexa-enabled home energy consumption trackers and a carbon monoxide detector, people familiar with the matter previously told Reuters.
