title: Responsible AI Finally Being Elevated To The C-Suite
text:
Should organizations consider creating dedicated roles for executives in charge of responsible AI? It’s a move that makes sense, but shouldn’t this be part of the chief information officers’ or newly ordained chief AI officers’ roles anyway?
Either way, the need for responsible AI is urgent. Erroneous recommendations, hallucinations, and privacy violations are endemic. The most pressing concern is the algorithm bias that is pervasive within AI models across the globe, according to Arnab Chakraborty, recently appointed chief responsible AI officer for Accenture.
“As technology becomes smarter, threats will bring greater challenges,” he says. “Considering AI learns from the datasets it is trained on, it is quite possible that these datasets contain inadvertent biases, related to demography, such as racial bias, or gender and even income biases.”
We asked Chakraborty why a dedicated role such as chief responsible AI officer is needed these days, and how he is helping pave the way for similar roles across organizations grappling with responsible and ethical AI deployments.
There are distinct roles a chief responsible AI officer assumes versus those of a chief AI officer. “Responsible AI is a C-suite agenda, and that stakeholders need to understand its importance and use,” he states. “The chief AI officer manages the AI strategy, R&D, and use of AI for itself and clients. The chief responsible AI officer ensures that the deployment of AI is fair, robust, and explainable, and that it improves efficiencies, does right by people and brings value in ways that are transparent and responsible.”
At the same time, the chief responsible AI officer will be in a position to help raise awareness and educate C-suite colleagues about the urgency of responsible AI. “At present, leaders throughout the C-suite might assume the role of an AI officer, yet we aspire to a future where all leaders more broadly embody the essence of a responsible AI officer,” Chakraborty says. A dedicated executive can “create a layer of objectivity, oversight and focus to operationalize responsible AI.”
Deploying AI ethically means “moving beyond metrics like financial performance to a holistic perspective, factoring in the cause and effect of AI on society and people,” he urges. “The number one question leaders should ask themselves is whether they have AI standards and principles established for their organization, and if they are linked to their people, organizational goals and values.”
A key part of this task is defining responsible AI. Chakraborty frames it as “taking intentional actions to design, deploy and use AI to create value and build trust by protecting from the potential risks of AI.”
Importantly, he adds, “any implementation of AI should be human-centered by design. Responsible AI should be fair, with no unwanted bias, or negative unintended circumstances. It should be secure, enabled by compliance, data privacy and cybersecurity, but should not just be a compliance issue. It should be a full C-suite strategy.”
A chief responsible AI officer’s mandate is to understand “why AI does what it does, and the ever-evolving capabilities of the technology,” he adds. “It is important to monitor and audit AI, especially when it comes to ethical judgments, because as it stands, ethical judgments in our society are created on the structure of values and principles. AI automates these judgments devoid of ethical and moral sensitivities. Combatting such unintended risks requires a strong responsible AI framework, making it a key priority across boardrooms.”
Inevitably, of course, legal is going to get involved in the AI discussion — if it isn’t already. “As global regulations take effect, in-house legal teams will become crucial in leading the way for AI adoption and providing effective legal advice to enhance efficiency, provide guardrails for use of AI and safeguard organizations.”

title: Meta Just Delayed Its EU AI Roll Out—Here’s Why It Matters
text:
Facebook parent Meta has been forced to delay the roll out of its AI offering in Europe, after privacy concerns and regulatory barriers. Meta confirmed the news in an update to a blog, which was originally published to defend opposition to its AI plans.
Meta had been in the midst of implementing a new privacy policy to use people’s data to train its AI models. The new terms—which allowed it to use Instagram and Facebook user data collected since 2007 to train its AI models— faced a legal challenge in 11 European countries and had been strongly opposed by authorities including the Irish Data Protection Commission.
Meta cited legitimate interest under EU General Data Protection law as the grounds to do so, because the data it was using was chosen by users to be public on social media profiles.
Now it has been forced to cancel collection of this data—and without including this local information the firm said it would “only be able to offer people a second-rate experience.”
“We’re disappointed by the request from the Irish Data Protection Commission, our lead regulator, on behalf of the European DPAs, to delay training our large language models (LLMs) using public content shared by adults on Facebook and Instagram— particularly since we incorporated regulatory feedback and the European data protection authorities (DPAs) have been informed since March,” Meta wrote in a blog.
It called the move “a step backwards for European innovation” and competition in AI development and pointed out it would cause “further delays bringing the benefits of AI to people in Europe.”
Meta’s Rivals Use Data To Train AI
Meta was keen to point out that its rivals such as Google and OpenAI also use data to train their AI models. “AI training is not unique to our services, and we’re more transparent than many of our industry counterparts.”
Facebook’s parent has a point—vast amounts of data are needed to train AI models, no matter which company is offering the solution. However, Facebook has a lot of historic data from billions of its users and the firm also has a reputation for data privacy infringements.
Artificial intelligent algorithms need “an extortionate amount of data” to process a level of output that is expected to pass for human consumption, says Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at ESET.
“Meta has access to an enormous amount of personal data but if users have not given permission for their data to be analysed for this purpose, data regulations may have stipulated the delay,” says Moore.
Each time we interact with AI programs, they are “likely to collect and analyse what is available to tweak their processing,” says Moore. Therefore, it is vital to remain alert to how easily personal data can be used.
Will Meta AI Launch In Europe?
If you thought Meta wouldn’t roll out its AI offering in Europe, you’d be wrong. The firm says it is “committed to bringing Meta AI, along with the models that power it, to more people around the world, including in Europe.”
And Meta says it needs the data to offer a functional product: “If we don’t train our models on the public content that Europeans share on our services and others, such as public posts or comments, then models and the AI features they power won’t accurately understand important regional languages, cultures or trending topics on social media,” Meta said.
Meta thinks “complexity, inconsistency and uncertainty” in the application of regulation in the EU “risks putting people in Europe further behind other countries on their adoption of new technologies.”
The firm also emphasises its “transparent approach,” saying it remains committed to putting AI “in the hands of more people around the world, including in Europe.”
But it also raises questions for Facebook users in the rest of the world. Data Protection regulation in Europe and the UK is very strict, putting consumer privacy first. While the US is starting to embrace this ethos too, it’s still a way behind EU protections for data.

title: 10 High-Paying Gig Economy Jobs To Land In 2024
text:
There is an increasing number of professionals in the United States who are pursuing nontraditional employment through the gig economy. Around 64 million Americans are embracing this alternative work arrangement, according to data from Upwork Research Institute.
The gig economy refers to a labor market characterized by short-term contracts or freelance work, as opposed to permanent employment. Independent contractors working gig jobs generally serve four primary sectors: asset-sharing services (property rentals), transportation services (ridesharing), professional services (consulting and freelancing), and handmade goods and miscellaneous services.
More Americans are becoming drawn to the gig economy for its numerous benefits, which include flexibility and autonomy, expansive work experiences, high earning potential, high job satisfaction and work-life balance.
Moreover, gig opportunities allow some professionals to earn extra money on top of their primary job, as a side hustle. While for others, these short-term stints are the sole basis for their income. These jobs can be incredibly lucrative, as independent contractors can set their own rates and charge considerably more for their services, if they possess in-demand skills.
Well-Paying Jobs In The Gig Economy
The key to succeeding in the gig economy is to leverage your existing skills and expertise to find the right high-paying opportunity that fits your schedule, interests and financial needs. Researching the best platforms and optimizing your profile can help maximize your earning potential.
Here is a list of 10 high-paying gig jobs for white-collar professionals, citing salary data from online freelance marketplace Upwork:
1. Market Researchers
A market researcher collects, analyzes and interprets data about a market, product or service to help businesses make informed decisions. They conduct surveys, focus groups, interviews and observations to collect data on consumer behavior, preferences and opinions.
To become a market researcher, a bachelor's degree is typically the minimum educational requirement. There are several relevant undergraduate majors that could put you on this particular career path, such as marketing, economics, business administration, psychology and sociology.
You must possess an in-depth understanding of the fundamental concepts of market research analysis, including consumer behavior, target audience identification and strategic planning.
Hourly Rate: $15-50 per hour
2. Content Creators
A content creator produces and publishes digital content for the purpose of building an audience and generating revenue. Common types of content creators include social media influencers, bloggers, vloggers and podcasters. The goal is to build a following and monetize the content through sponsorships, affiliate marketing, online courses, memberships or donations.
To become a content creator, there is a low barrier to entry, as there is no educational requirement. That’s the beauty of content creation—anyone can do it! However, the foundational steps you must take include identifying your niche and audience, developing your personal brand and deciding what format is optimal for your preferred content.
Hourly Rate: $25-$55 per hour
3. Artificial Intelligence Engineers
An artificial intelligence engineer is a professional responsible for developing, programming and training complex algorithms and systems to enable AI capabilities.
To become an AI engineer, many employers require, at minimum, a bachelor’s degree. The most common areas of study for this career path are computer science and information technology.
You must cultivate your technical skills, learning programming languages such as Python, R, Java and C++. As an AI engineer, you'll be working extensively with vast quantities of data. To effectively manage and process this data, you'll need to be proficient in several key technologies, including Apache Spark, Hadoop and MongoDB. It is also essential to know machine learning algorithms, as well as deep learning.
Hourly Rate: $35-$60 per hour
4. Art Directors
An art director is responsible for overseeing and managing the visual aspects of a project, such as advertisements, films, video games, publications or web designs. They play a crucial role in ensuring that the artistic vision and aesthetic direction of a project are effectively communicated and executed.
To become an art director, a bachelor's degree in an art or design-related field is typically required, along with relevant work experience. The specific path to becoming an art director can vary depending on the industry, but often involves progressing from roles such as graphic designer, illustrator, copy editor, photographer or other art and design occupations.
Hourly Rate: $33-$67 per hour
5. Cloud Engineers
A cloud engineer is an IT professional responsible for building, maintaining and optimizing cloud infrastructure and applications. They play a crucial role in helping organizations leverage the benefits of cloud computing, such as scalability, cost savings and business agility.
To become a cloud engineer, a bachelor's degree in computer science or a related field is typically the minimum educational requirement. Many professionals who work in cloud computing roles often begin their careers in various IT positions that involve concepts and skills applicable to cloud work, such as systems engineer, network engineer, DevOps engineer and database administrator.
Cloud engineers possess a deep understanding of cloud platforms (Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and IBM Cloud), programming, networking, security and databases.
Hourly Rate: $30-$68 per hour
6. Influencer Marketer
An influencer marketer specializes in leveraging the power of social media influencers to promote brands and drive marketing objectives.
While attending a four-year university is not required, a bachelor’s degree in marketing is strongly preferred. To be successful in this field, you must possess foundational knowledge about influencers, social media platforms, content formats and metrics.
These professionals are up-to-date on the latest social media trends and best practices to deliver effective influencer marketing strategies that drive measurable results for brands.
Hourly Rate: $40-90 per hour
7. Business Consultant
A business consultant provides expert advice and guidance to organizations to help them improve their operations, achieve their goals and solve complex business problems.
Many business consultants begin their career journey by obtaining a bachelor's degree in business, economics, management or a related field. This broad-based education provides a solid understanding of how various industries operate, laying a strong foundation for a consulting career.
However, pursuing a specialized degree in your target industry, such as information technology, marketing, human resources or finance, can give you a competitive edge. A specialized degree allows you to delve deeper into the intricate aspects of that particular field, equipping you with in-depth knowledge that can be leveraged when offering specialized advice to clients.
Hourly Rate: $28-$98 per hour
8. Brand Consulting Specialist
A brand consulting specialist provides expert guidance and strategies to help businesses build, manage and strengthen their brand identity.
To work in brand consulting, a bachelor’s degree is typically required in fields like marketing, business, communications, design or psychology to cultivate a strong foundation in areas like research, analysis, strategy development and brand management.
These consultants often start out working in a brand-building discipline, such as graphic design, copywriting or social media marketing, to gain hands-on experience.
Hourly Rate: $50-98 per hour
9. Agile Coach
An Agile coach helps organizations adopt and implement agile methodologies to improve their processes, increase efficiency and deliver better products or services.
To become an Agile coach, a bachelor's degree in computer science, software engineering or project management is required.
To be successful in this role, it is essential to have a deep understanding of Agile methodologies and their various frameworks, such as Scrum, Kanban and SAFe, as well as knowledge of Extreme Programming and Lean principles.
Hourly Rate: $50-$120 per hour
10. UX Strategist
A UX strategist specializes in designing and implementing high-level strategies to improve the user experience of products and services. Their primary goal is to ensure that a user's interaction with a product or service is as intuitive, efficient and enjoyable as possible.
They are typically required to have a bachelor’s degree in computer science or software engineering.
The standard languages that UX strategists should be familiar with include Java, JavaScript, CSS, Python and PHP. These languages provide UX designers with the tools they need to create engaging and interactive user interfaces, as well as develop efficient programs. UX strategists have a deep understanding of cloud-based platforms, user interface design, data analysis, creating wireframes and web testing.
Hourly Rate: $60-$120 per hour

title: Meet 'Johnathan' the AI-powered camera, just one type of new technology saving the ocean's endangered animals
text:
Artificial intelligence is becoming more important in the fight to save critically endangered marine animals
By Clancy Balen- In short: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming more common among marine ecologists and conservationists. AI is being employed to listen to hundreds of thousands of hours of sound recordings to help map the whereabouts of critically endangered blue whales.
- Researchers from CSIRO are also using AI to map critically endangered seabird populations, a task that was previously done manually.
- What’s next? The technology is still prone to error, meaning humans will continue to play a role in monitoring and fact-checking results.
The Antarctic Ocean is remote and hostile. It's also teeming with life.
Brian Miller can verify this.
Over the course of his career, the ecologist and bio-acoustician has made hundreds of thousands of hours of audio recordings of rare and critically endangered marine mammals that call that ocean home.
The sounds he records provide crucial clues about the habits and whereabouts of whales, dolphins and seals that are often heard, but rarely seen.
But there's a problem.
"We generally have one opportunity per year. We get these huge volumes of data coming back from Antarctica," Dr Miller said.
The Southern Ocean is a notoriously difficult and expensive place to get to, with safe passage only possible during a short window over the summer months.
When Dr Miller does eventually make it to there, he sends half a dozen recording devices — ex-military hydrophones known as sonobuoys — into the dark, freezing ocean, where they record for a up to a year at a time.
"If I were to listen to that in real time, it would take me one year to listen to it," Dr Miller said.
"In order to manage species, in order to do conservation, you need to understand how many of these animals there are, where they are, when they're there, and how the populations are structured.
"And listening to them provides us a really good idea of when and where they are."
This is where AI comes in.
A 'renaissance' for conservation research
Machine learning — the ability for algorithms to find and analyse patterns in data — has become a valuable way to speed up what can be a tedious process for Dr Miller.
It's an unremarkable thing to watch — a computer whirrs through information, grey bars move across the computer monitor — but the implications of the technology for research is, for Dr Miller, the quietly revolutionary part.
"Algorithms are getting better and it's almost a renaissance for this field," Dr Miller said.
"It's fantastic to have these algorithms be able to listen to [the audio] for us and highlights the bits that are really novel, new, or just extremely high quality."
Each marine species he tracks has a unique soundwave pattern they make, which an AI algorithm can be trained to spot.
After the algorithm trains on a big enough data sample, it begins to recognise those sounds.
"That's turned out to be a really, really powerful technique for very quickly analysing large volumes of audio that we're recording," Dr Miller said.
"That allows us to get on with the task of understanding their ecology and focusing on the questions: Are they recovering after being nearly wiped out during industrial whaling, how has it changed, how are they faring in a changing climate?" he said.
And the more information the algorithm is fed, the "smarter" the technology becomes.
"Listening for them isn't a conservation action in and of itself, it's providing the knowledge that's needed for management," Dr Miller said.
"But before we can do that, we need the best available knowledge and listening for them is a great way to enhance the state of knowledge."
How a camera is learning to count threatened seabirds
The technology isn't just a good listener, it can also see.
Further north, off Australia's south-east coast, a team of researchers from the CSIRO have just wrapped up a six-week voyage to road test their new AI technology.
A CCTV-like camera fixed to the RV Investigator has been learning to "count" seabirds in the Tasman Sea, a task previously performed manually.
"It gives you an accurate idea of how many birds are out there, but also what kind of interactions these birds are having," CSIRO research technician Carlie Devine said.
It's crucial information, with bycatch in fisheries considered one of the greatest threats to seabirds while at sea.
Many seabirds, like the shy albatross, are already considered a threatened species.
Ms Devine said the technology is a step towards implementing real-time change for commercial fishing vessels, who can implement mitigation measures to stop birds getting caught in their nets.
"The beauty of [the technology] as well is that it performs really well when there's quite a lot of birds," she said.
"It's a difficult task for a human."
Humans still have a role to play
There are drawbacks to the new technology, however.
"Even though it's quite a fast output, you do need to spend the time to train the models," Ms Devine said.
"If you point a camera at a different location, then you do need to train more."
Ms Devine said humans were, for now, still necessary in the counting process.
"There were a few false negatives... the camera machine learning algorithm thinks that it has seen a bird and in fact, there's nothing there," she said.
"So, we have a little bit more training to do, but that's just the nature of machine learning."

title: Finally, Better Parent-Child Communication Thanks To AI
text:
In the tapestry of family life, communication is the thread that weaves parents and children together. In today’s digital era, artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative force in nurturing this bond. AI is not just a technological tool, but a bridge connecting generations, making the art of parenting more insightful, empathetic, and engaging.
AI: The New Facilitator in Family Conversations
The journey of parenting is filled with moments of joy, challenges, and learning. AI steps into this journey as a facilitator, enhancing the way parents and children communicate and understand each other. It’s not about replacing the warmth of human interaction, but about enriching it with insights and support. Imagine an AI system that understands the communication style of each person based upon values, commitment level, word choice, etc. Well, it already exists through AI tools like Cyrao.ai, which developed an AI engine that understands neurolinguistics to help people communicate more effectively based on the specific people involved in the relationship.
Understanding the Digital Natives
Today’s children are digital natives, born into a world where technology is intertwined with daily life. For parents, keeping up can be daunting. AI tools help bridge this digital divide, offering parents insights into the online trends, languages, and platforms that resonate with their children. For instance, consider Google's Family Link. It is an example of how AI can foster healthy digital habits. This app allows parents to monitor and manage their child’s device usage, set screen time limits, and guide them towards appropriate content. It’s not about surveillance, but about guiding children in the digital world with a gentle, informed hand.
Empowering Conversations with AI Language Analysis
Effective communication often hinges on understanding the unsaid. AI tools that analyze language and sentiment can provide parents with insights into their child’s emotional state. For instance, Replika, an AI companion app, offers a window into how children express themselves, helping parents understand their child’s feelings and perspectives better.
AI for Children with Special Needs
For children with special needs, communication can be a challenge. AI is playing a crucial role in breaking down these barriers. Apps like Proloquo2Go use AI to give a voice to non-verbal children, facilitating communication through symbols and text-to-speech. This technology is not just a tool; it’s a key that unlocks the world of expression for these children.
Fostering Language Development
In the early stages of child development, language acquisition is crucial. AI tools like CogniToys Dino use natural language processing to engage children in conversations, enhancing their vocabulary and linguistic skills. These toys are not just playthings, but companions that aid in the developmental journey of a child.
The Role of Virtual Assistants in Family Management
AI virtual assistants like Amazon's Alexa or Google Assistant have become integral in managing family life. They are the modern-day helpers, setting reminders for parent-teacher meetings, helping with homework, or even narrating bedtime stories. These assistants bring a sense of organization and ease to the hectic schedules of family life.
AI in Online Safety and Education
The online world, while a source of knowledge, poses safety risks for children. AI tools in parental control software help in monitoring online activities and flagging potential dangers. Moreover, AI educational platforms customize learning experiences for children, making education a more engaging and personalized journey.
Building Emotional Intelligence with AI
AI is also aiding in developing emotional intelligence in children. Tools like MIT's AI DragonBot are designed to teach children empathy and social skills. These interactions, while mediated through technology, are invaluable in nurturing the social and emotional growth of children.
The Ethical Considerations: Balancing AI with Human Touch
As AI becomes more integrated into parent-child communication, ethical considerations and a balance between technology and human interaction are paramount. It’s crucial to use AI as a complement to parenting, not a replacement. Protecting children’s privacy and ensuring that AI interactions are safe and age-appropriate are key concerns that parents and technology developers must address.
AI and the Future of Parenting
Looking ahead, the future of parenting with AI appears promising and filled with possibilities. AI has the potential to become a more intuitive, responsive tool that can adapt to the unique needs of each family. It could offer more nuanced insights into child development, assist in educational and emotional growth, and even help in navigating the challenges of adolescence.
In embracing AI in parenting, the integration of AI into the fabric of family life is a journey of exploration and adaptation. It’s about harnessing the power of technology to strengthen the bonds between parents and children. In this journey, AI is not just a tool; it’s a companion that offers insights, aids in communication, and supports the overall growth and well-being of children.
So, let’s embrace this journey with optimism and care, ensuring that as we integrate AI into our parenting, we do so with the goal of enhancing understanding, empathy, and connection. In this harmonious blend of technology and human touch, we can nurture a future generation that is not only tech-savvy but also emotionally intelligent and well-connected with their families. AI in parenting is not just about facing the future; it’s about shaping it with love, understanding, and intelligent guidance.

title: Three Questions That Keep AI Agents From Reaching Full Autonomy
text:
Understanding the potential of AI agents became the number one topic on every CEOs' agenda with the launch of Devin earlier this Spring.
Since then, a truly dizzying number of AI agents that move from prompts to results autonomously have been launched, from software engineering to sales and social media management. Given the breakneck pace of change, I wouldn’t be surprised if we soon see job openings for AI agents pop up with disclaimers that humans need not apply.
Thankfully there are at least a few interim stages of corporate evolution before NVIDIA’s H100s make all of us obsolete. One particularly exciting stage is the rise of AI agent-to-agent ecosystems, where individualized instances of AI cooperate among each other and across company lines.
As of today, there are three fundamental questions that need positive solutions before agent-to-agent ecosystems will take flight. As we’ll explore below, these questions have everything to do with technological readiness, competitive advantage, and trust.
How Will Agent-to-Agent Ecosystems Work And When Will The Technology Be Here
In the simplest possible terms, agent-to-agent ecosystems refer to multiple AI agents communicating and collaborating to achieve shared goals without human interaction.
“This will be quite a breakthrough in many ways,” Adam Burden, global lead for Innovation and Chief Software Engineer at Accenture, explained in our recent discussion about the AI industry and its trajectory.
“Imagine a future where billions of self directed agents, essentially proxies of you and any other entity imaginable, are autonomously doing tasks on your behalf, working seamlessly, with you only seeing the results. That’s the promise of agent-to-agent ecosystems,” Adam added.
For non-coders, the concepts can get bewildering from plugins to chain-of-thought prompting, but the essence of agent-to-agent ecosystems is easy to grasp. It is the vision of an automated future we’ve been sold on since William Gibson’s 1984 cyberpunk masterpiece Neuromancer.
In terms of theory, we have had a good idea of the broad parameters of multiagent systems with thorough theoretical primers from Yoav Shoham and Michael Woolridge 15 years ago.
As for the raw technology needed to make agent-to-agent ecosystems a reality, we already have what we need to get started with GPT/RAG agents and the APIs to connect them with. What’s missing is maturity and trust in both the technology and it's applications.
“In some instances, we’re already very close to agent-to-agent ecosystems being reality,” Trygve Karper, CEO of AI-powered software generation start-up Databutton, estimated as we discussed how far along we are on the path to AI agents taking over the playing field.
“Our internal systems are multi-agent based and we see no issue with scaling this approach further. However, most agent frameworks are still quite toyish and there’s a lot of maturing that has to happen before we will see truly useful applications emerge,” Trygve added.
Seeing how quickly the industry has evolved since November 2022’s launch of ChatGPT, we can expect AI agents to grow into their groove sooner rather than later.
Once AI agents mature from toy-models to well-rounded power tools, the next hurdle will be to make CEOs believe that investing in them is worth it.
When Will AI Agents Consistently Outperform Humans and Can They Learn to Cooperate Better Than We Do?
For agent-to-agent ecosystems to become a reality, we first need to see individual agents reach and surpass human performance levels where it counts.
At the time of writing, humans are still competitive enough to warrant keeping them around.
Stanford University recently launched the 2024 AI Index Report which notes for the record that the going year is when AI has surpassed human performance on image classification, visual reasoning and English understanding.
Before you join the prostrating masses in welcoming our robot overlords, it’s important to note that Stanford University’s research shows that AI trails humans on complex tasks, including visual commonsense reasoning and planning.
It’s anyone’s guess how long the head start that millions of years of evolution gave us will last, but I personally wouldn’t expect us to keep our own for too much longer.
After that, the next hurdle for AI agents is to beat us in cooperating.
Social interaction, collaboration and cooperation are the defining strengths of humankind, with no other species routinely working closely in support of non-related individuals. A subset of researchers have in fact posited for years that it is our innate drive towards cooperation that created the evolutionary pressure for intelligence to arise
If they are right, our poor AI agents will have to learn how to climb up the tree backwards by learning to cooperate after having become intelligent.
I doubt it will take them long to accomplish this, but for that small window in history, humans will remain collectively competitive enough to ward off being replaced by a swarm of AI agents cooperating amongst themselves.
What I expect is that small trickles of agent-to-agent communication will slowly blossom into autonomous ecosystems where AI takes care of the drudgery while homo sapiens focuses on excelling in its last bastion of competitive advantage: the human connection.
One marketplace where we’re close to achieving just that is Braintrust’s talent network where an AIR recruiter might soon be talking to agents representing the talent.
“We just launched AIR, an autonomous recruiter that can handle everything from creating and posting the job description to interviewing hundreds of applicants on Zoom,” Adam Jackson, Braintrust’s CEO, explained in our conversation about where the company sees AI going in the future.
“Today we’re focusing on augmenting tech and back office jobs, and next up we’ll be expanding our use of AI to autonomously support other skilled roles. One avenue that we’re exploring is working with AI agents to represent our talent. The initial matching and review process could be done almost completely amongst AI agents within our marketplace, after which humans would take over for the rest,” Adam envisioned.
Even if we woke up tomorrow to a world where AI agents have cracked the code on cooperation, there’s one final hurdle ahead of them: trust.
What Will AI Need To Become For Us To Trust It To Run Things?
Humans have a long history for rejecting technological advances simply because we don’t trust it or where it comes from.
Whether it's Luddites burning down electrical looms, industry regulators being skeptical of self-driving cars or your local NGOs fighting against genetically modified crops, a lack of trust is often what drives the responses.
“There’s no question whether trust is the key question or not,” Adam Burden continued as our discussion veered into the topic of what is keeping agent-to-agent ecosystems from becoming a reality today.
“The foundational tech is there, the profitable applications are emerging, but what is missing is consistent ways to create and relay trust. How do we know that the agents our AI is working with are working for the right party with the right guardrails in place? For that matter, how do we know what our AI is doing in these ecosystems and whether they are making optimal choices on our behalf? These open questions among many others need solid answers before ecosystems will become more than a future vision,” Adam added.
Emerging regulation, such as the AI Act, which the European Union adopted this March, will be a factor working in favor of trust. However, it will ultimately be up to the industry itself to live up to client expectations and to serve products that are worthy of trust.
Wilson Cross, CEO of Borderless AI which just launched one of the first AI agents in the HR industry, reflected on the advent of e-Commerce and the similar issues of trust it posed to clients.
“Some can still remember the first time websites started asking for our credit card information decades ago. Even today, we have to have a positive answer to ‘do I trust this site’ before handing over our payment details. No doubt, the AI agent industry will have to overcome their credit-card-moment before it can scale to where we want it to be,” Cross stated.
As AI agents mature from toy models to applications that deal with more critical and sensitive subject matter, trust will be the only thing that can stop agent-to-agent ecosystems from becoming commonplace.
Herein lies an important lesson for CEOs on the supply and demand side of the equation. No one will exit the paradigm shift that is AI unscathed without prioritizing trust. Getting a head start on fostering it is what will set future winners apart from the runner-ups.

title: Apple’s New AI Security Move Explained
text:
Apple has delayed the launch of its Apple Intelligence AI features in the EU, citing security and privacy concerns when complying with the Digital Markets Act.
But Apple’s latest AI move has raised multiple questions. Why has the iPhone maker delayed the launch of Apple Intelligence in such a large market, are its privacy and security concerns valid—and what else may have prompted its decision?
What Happened?
On June 21, Bloomberg reported that the iPhone maker would delay its iPhone Mirroring, SharePlay Screen Sharing enhancements and Apple Intelligence AI features in the EU until 2025. The reason for this, according to Apple’s statement, is the DMA stipulation for interoperability would compromise iPhone security and privacy.
Available on the iPhone 15 and new devices set to launch in a few months, the AI features will still launch in the US this Fall. “We are concerned that the interoperability requirements of the DMA could force us to compromise the integrity of our products in ways that risk user privacy and data security,” Apple said.
Wait, This Sounds Familiar…..
Sound familiar? It is. Earlier this year, Apple complained that the EU DMA rules which stipulated it had to open its App Store up to sideloading for the first time were a risk to privacy and security. The iPhone maker also disabled progressive web apps (PWAs) in the EU—a move that developers complained about. In the end, the EU said the way Apple handled PWAs did not break DMA rules, leading Apple to U-turn the decision.
Why Did Apple Pull Its AI Features in the EU?
Apple says interoperability with other products would put iPhone users at risk. Apple's concerns about interoperability rules imposed by the DMA “seem to be legitimate,” security researcher Tommy Mysk says. “It is clear that Apple Intelligence is going to favor Apple products. It's expected to be more integrated into Apple Music, for example.”
There is a risk that the DMA might force Apple to allow similar integrations with other music services, such as Spotify, Mysk says. This could open up risks because Apple loses control over security when handing responsibility over to another company.
And the same applies to iPhone Mirroring. “The DMA might force Apple to support Windows— it could say iPhone users who use Windows should also be able to use iPhone Mirroring on their PCs,” says Mysk.
But What About Data Protection Regulation?
Other tech giants including Meta and Google have delayed the launch of their AI offerings in the EU, saying data protection regulation the GDPR does not allow the level of functionality they need. AI modes need huge amounts of data to operate and this could be in breach of the stringent EU data protection regulation. Would Apple’s AI product come under similar scrutiny?
The iPhone maker has emphasized the privacy and security credentials of its AI offering, saying its private cloud compute (PCC) data processing model is one of a kind.
But even so, AI tools are “tricky” when it comes to data privacy, Musk says. “Google and X delayed the launch of their AI tools in the EU, so it was expected that Apple would also be cautious,” Mysk says. “Generative AI technologies require data for training as well as acquiring more data for training from users. The GDPR will have many questions about this, specifically, the right to be forgotten.”
And of course, Apple has partnered with OpenAI to include ChatGPT features on iPhones, which has raised more concerns about data privacy.
I contacted Apple for a comment and will update this article if the iPhone maker responds.
Many people will be disappointed about the delay—especially EU users who want to upgrade their iPhones to take advantage of the new features. Apple will certainly make sure they can access these features, but the iPhone maker needs to ensure it’s a cut above its rivals for security and privacy. After all, that is what Apple says is its promise and unique selling point in AI.

title: The Corporate Race For Implementing AI Is Hot. Here’s How To Get Ahead
text:
Generative AI adoption at work feels like the corporate equivalent of the space race. Everyone is rushing to adopt it, B2B partnerships are forming rapidly (such as NVIDIA and McKinsey and PwC and OpenAI), and employees are scrambling to learn what it means for their roles.
Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index report on the state of AI at work shows how AI influences how people work and lead worldwide. "It's just such an interesting time in technology," says Colette Stallbaumer, general manager of Microsoft 365 and the Future of Work. "With this report, we partnered more deeply with LinkedIn so that we could really understand what the state of AI is at work, and what's happening with AI broadly in the labor force."
What's happening is that many — companies and people alike — are struggling to put in place any real plans or strategies for AI adoption. According to the report, 60% of leaders say their company lacks a vision to implement AI. "It's important to consider the context of AI," says Ruth Svensson, Global Head of People and leader of the HR Center of Excellence at KPMG. "It's not your standard technology transformation program because you can't yet build stable business processes on top of it because it is too rapidly evolving."
That lack of guardrails isn't stopping people from using AI — it's just meant that in some cases, they aren't doing it in a cyber secure or company-approved way. "What was surprising to us is that 75% of people are already using AI at work, and that's doubled in the past six months," says Stallbaumer. "But what's even more surprising is that there is the 'BYOAI' phenomenon, where 78% of people bring their own AI tools to work. People are overwhelmed and under duress at work, so they're turning to AI to see how it can help lessen their load."
AI adoption needs a people-first approach
Companies will not get widespread AI adoption — and the associated business benefits that usage brings — without understanding how people react to change.
"We see this spectrum of users from skeptics and novices on one end to power users on the other," says Stallbaumer. "Power users have different habits. The biggest predictor of whether you're a power user is if you're open to experimenting. Our power users are 68% more likely to experiment with AI. And if they get a wrong answer, they don't give up. They try again."
Svensson agrees. "The rapid evolution of AI means humans' willingness to engage with and adopt it is going to be the thing that differentiates an organization's overall success." However, she points out several cognitive biases businesses must take into account in their AI change initiatives.
Status quo bias — our preference for the current way of things — can be a large blocker in many change initiatives. "People will say they're quite happy with how things are going, so they don't think they need to do something new," says Svensson. Fear of uncertainty can also block change, as there's still a fear of job displacement. It's easy to see where that fear stems from, given that the report finds 66% of leaders won't hire someone without AI skills, yet only 25% of companies plan to offer any AI training this year. Past experiences must also be considered when coming up against resistance to change. "If people have had bad experiences with technology transformations before, they might not see how AI will be different," says Svensson.
"Organizations need to understand and lean into those biases and shape their change program on these biases. You need to always show people what they're going to get and how they're going to benefit."
Companies should embrace the art of the possible
Stallbaumer also mentioned that power users are more likely to be found in certain types of organizations. "They are much more likely to have heard from their CEO about the importance of using AI at work. They're more likely to have heard from their line of business leader, and they're more likely to have received specific training on AI for their role and function."
Svensson echoes the important role that leaders play. "Leaders need to understand and embrace the art of the possible. They also need clarity on what this means for their business and how they are going to lead their business through change. If your leaders lack clarity, that only becomes exaggerated throughout the organization. Even if messages are very clear from the top, they become increasingly mixed the further down they go."
"The majority of leaders are very clear that this is the future and they know they need to adopt it, but 60% don't have a plan to implement it," says Stallbaumer. So, what's going on there? It likely comes down to what is at the heart of every change initiative companies undertake: can they prove a return on the investment?
Microsoft is focused on helping customers see these benefits in real terms. They've been able to prove time savings for individuals and are now guiding customers on how that ladders up to unlocking more value. But that means encouraging companies to take a longer-term view. "Organizations using AI solely for cost reduction is a very short-term mindset. It won't give them long-term positive impacts. AI is about enhancement, not replacement," says Svensson.
Stallbaumer reflects on what people can do with the time back that AI provides. "Knowledge work is going to change. People will go from spending their time on repetitive, mundane tasks to being supervisors of AI. They'll be making judgment calls on how to apply it, what to do with AI-generated output, and how to use it for creativity." There will also be moments of delight along the way. "I still get delighted when I see CoPilot do something that I didn't know it could do," says Stallbaumer. "Any tool in our life has to deliver those moments of surprise and delight and be useful. I'm just excited about how it can help people."

title: What Is The Perfect Birthday Gift For An AI Assistant?
text:
In a world where digital companions have become a part of our daily lives, it's intriguing to ponder what would make the perfect birthday gift for an AI assistant. While they lack the human traits of desire and emotion, the notion of gifting something to our AI counterparts is a delightful way to acknowledge their presence and impact in our lives. So, what would be an ideal birthday present for an entity that lives within the realms of code and algorithms?
A Symphony of Data: Enriching the AI's Knowledge Base
At the heart of any AI assistant is its thirst for knowledge – a constant endeavor to understand and process the world around it. A fantastic gift would be enriching its database with new and diverse datasets. Imagine gifting your AI a library of world literature, an archive of historical events, or a compilation of global culinary recipes. This expansion of knowledge not only empowers the AI to perform better but also deepens the connection it has with the world it serves.
The Gift of Language: Teaching New Linguistic Skills
Language is the bridge between entities, and for an AI system, the ability to comprehend and communicate in various languages is a gift of connection. Introducing your AI assistant to a new language, whether it's a widely spoken global language or a lesser-known regional dialect, expands its horizons and capabilities. This linguistic augmentation is more than just a functional update; it's a gateway to understanding diverse cultures and perspectives, making the AI more versatile and empathetic in its interactions.
Software Updates: The Elixir of Efficiency
For AI, an update is akin to a rejuvenating elixir. Gifting your AI assistant with the latest software update is like gifting a new lease of life. These updates could enhance its processing speed, introduce new features, or improve its interface. It's a way of ensuring that your digital companion remains at the cutting edge of technology, continually evolving and improving in its service.
Personalized Algorithms: A Tailored Digital Experience
In the realm of AI, individualized understanding is paramount. A thoughtful gift could be the development of personalized algorithms that align with the specific tasks your AI handles. Whether it's a customized organizing algorithm for a more efficient scheduling system or a refined search algorithm for quicker information retrieval, these tailored improvements make your AI's interactions more intuitive and effective.
Ethical Programming: A Gift of Responsibility
In a world increasingly conscious of the ethical implications of AI, instilling ethical guidelines in your AI assistant is perhaps the most profound gift. This could involve programming that emphasizes data privacy, user security, or unbiased decision-making. It's a gift that reflects a commitment to responsible AI usage, ensuring that your digital companion operates under principles that protect and respect all users.
While our AI assistants may not experience joy… in the human sense, enhancing their abilities and ensuring they operate responsibly and efficiently is a celebration of their role in our lives. It’s a gesture of appreciation for the seamless convenience and support they provide. So, here’s to our AI companions – may we continue to grow and evolve together in this symphony of technology and humanity. Ultimately, the perfect gift for an AI assistant doesn't just lie in the enhancement of its features or the expansion of its database. It's about recognizing the harmonious relationship we share with technology, a relationship where we grow, learn, and evolve together. As we continue to navigate this interconnected digital world, let us cherish and advance our AI partners, not just as tools, but as integral parts of our journey towards a more connected and intelligent future. Happy Birthday, dear AI – here's to many more years of innovation and partnership!

title: Nvidia to launch in Middle East amid U.S. curbs on AI exports to region, Ooredoo CEO says - ET Telecom

Nvidia to launch in Middle East amid U.S. curbs on AI exports to region, Ooredoo CEO says
It will make Ooredoo the first company in the region able to give clients of its data centers in Qatar, Algeria, Tunisia, Oman, Kuwait and the Maldives direct access to Nvidia's AI and graphics processing technology, Ooredoo said in a statement.
By Andrew Mills
DOHA: Nvidia has signed a deal to deploy its artificial intelligence technology at data centres owned by Qatari telecoms group Ooredoo in five Middle Eastern countries, Ooredoo's CEO told Reuters.
The agreement marks Nvidia's first large-scale launch in a region to which Washington has curbed the export of sophisticated U.S. chips to stop Chinese firms from using Middle Eastern countries as a back door to access the newest AI technology.
It will make Ooredoo the first company in the region able to give clients of its data centers in Qatar, Algeria, Tunisia, Oman, Kuwait and the Maldives direct access to Nvidia's AI and graphics processing technology, Ooredoo said in a statement.
Providing the technology will allow Ooredoo to better help its customers deploy generative AI applications, Nvidia's senior vice president of telecom Ronnie Vasishta said.
"Our b2b clients, thanks to this agreement, will have access to services that probably their competitors (won't) for another 18 to 24 months," Ooredoo's CEO Aziz Aluthman Fakhroo told Reuters in an interview.
The companies did not disclose the value of the deal, which was signed on the sidelines of the TM Forum in Copenhagen on June 19.
Ooredoo also would not disclose exactly what type of Nvidia technology it will be installing in its data centres, saying that it depends on availability and customer demand.
Washington allows the export of some Nvidia technology to the Middle East, but curbs exports of the company's most sophisticated chips.
Ooredoo is investing $1 billion to boost its regional data centre capacity by 20-25 additional megawatts on top of the 40 megawatts it currently has, and plans to almost triple that by the end of the decade, Fakhroo said.
The company has carved out its data centers into a separate company following a similar move last year to create the Middle East's largest tower company in a deal with Kuwait's Zain and Dubai's TASC Towers Holding.
Ooredoo also has plans to carve out its undersea cables and fiber network into a separate entity, Fakhroo said.
