title: Council Post: Redefining Retirement: The Impact Of Fully Digitized Annuities In The Age Of AI And Blockchain
text:
Santiago Vinoth Jeyaseelan is VP of Product Management & Design at Gainbridge, an insurtech company revolutionizing the annuity industry.
In today's quickly changing financial services industry, digitizing annuity products represents a tremendous opportunity to reshape retirement planning and financial security for future generations. By incorporating advanced technologies like artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain, the annuities sector is poised to transform how these financial products are handled, tailored and bought, bringing in a new era of efficiency, security and user engagement.
The Promise Of Accessibility And Inclusion
The shift to digital annuities represents a new era of convenience and control in financial planning. Often burdened by complex paperwork and unclear processes, traditional annuity products can be overwhelming for many. Digital annuities simplify the investment process through user-friendly online platforms, making it accessible to a wider audience.
According to research from the Insured Retirement Institute (IRI), improving access to retirement planning tools significantly increases participation rates, particularly among younger and underserved demographics. It also found that consumers prioritize retirement income and asset protection more than growth. This democratization and consumer expectation are essential for fostering an inclusive and strong financial future.
Enhanced Personalization With AI
Artificial intelligence is playing an increasingly important role in personalizing retirement planning. By utilizing AI's data analysis and predictive modeling capabilities, annuity providers can create personalized investment strategies that align with an individual's financial objectives, risk tolerance and life circumstances. According to a report by Accenture, AI has the potential to improve customer experiences by offering more relevant and personalized advice, resulting in greater satisfaction and loyalty. Furthermore, AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants provide 24/7 support, making the annuities market more accessible and user-friendly.
A great case study of AI in action is how New York Life recently began implementing AI to improve its marketing efforts, help make call center representatives and agents more productive and aid in underwriting and predictive modeling. Generative AI is helping New York Life find a form or answer to a policyholder question much faster than traditional means, leading to increased customer satisfaction scores and reduced churn rates.
Blockchain: A New Paradigm For Security And Transparency
Blockchain technology could provide unmatched security and transparency to annuity contracts. By storing annuity contracts on a decentralized ledger, blockchain ensures that the details of an agreement are unchangeable and visible to all parties involved. This reduces the potential for fraud and simplifies claims and payouts, as smart contracts can automatically carry out transactions based on predetermined conditions. According to Congruent, blockchain can enhance trust in financial transactions, a crucial element in long-term retirement planning.
AXA, a French insurance giant, utilized blockchain technology to develop Fizzy, a blockchain-based insurance platform that automatically processes claims in the event of flight delays. This technology could also be adapted for annuities, using smart contracts to guarantee that payments and other contract terms are fulfilled without manual intervention. The transparency and security blockchain offers have enhanced customer confidence and optimized operational efficiency. Fizzy's achievements demonstrate the potential for blockchain to revolutionize conventional insurance and annuity contract agreements.
Synergy Between AI And Blockchain
The fusion of AI and blockchain can potentially revolutionize the annuity industry. AI can analyze large datasets to create annuities tailored to individuals' specific needs, while blockchain can securely manage the entire lifecycle of these contracts. This combination can result in the development of highly personalized and secure financial products. For instance, AI-generated insights can customize annuity offerings to an individual's unique profile, while blockchain guarantees the integrity and security of these financial instruments.
Operational Efficiency And Cost Reduction
Digitizing annuities can streamline operations and reduce administrative burdens, lowering consumer fees and higher provider returns. Digitization can increase accessibility, improve searchability, improve collaboration and digital competition, enhance document processing, reduce storage costs, improve document retention and increase security. These increased efficiencies applied to annuities make them more attractive and enable access to a broader population.
Challenges And Future Directions
Despite the considerable advantages, the journey toward fully digitized annuities poses challenges. The industry has relied on traditional distribution models, which still show 20% plus growth. So, the shift toward digitization and the desire to adopt AI due to privacy and intellectual property concerns are big blockers for the industry to overcome. These challenges must be addressed to ensure fair access and protect consumer assets. Regulatory bodies must also adjust to the rapid pace of technological advancements by creating policies that promote innovation while safeguarding consumers.
The Road Ahead
As we look to the future, I think it will be a transformative moment when we fully integrate AI and blockchain into the annuities sector. The Covid-19 pandemic accelerated the digital revolution in financial services, highlighting the need for flexible, secure, personalized financial products. Annuities, which are crucial for retirement planning, stand to benefit significantly from these technological advancements. As these technologies evolve, their adoption in the annuities market will likely bring revolutionary changes, empowering individuals to more confidently and easily navigate their financial futures.
In conclusion, digitizing annuities and using AI and blockchain technology offers a future where retirement planning focuses on achieving personalized financial goals and ensuring financial security that evolves with each individual. The potential advantages for consumers and the industry are substantial, signaling a future where retirement planning is accessible, flexible and secure for all. It is time to welcome this change and strive for a more inclusive and innovative financial future.

title: ChatGPT Is Biased Against Resumes Mentioning Disability, Research Shows
text:
The practice of recruiters deploying artificial intelligence to scan and sort candidate resumes has become fairly common over the past few years. AI makes such tasks, previously undertaken by HR staff, more streamlined and efficient by being able to summarize large quantities of data, highlight desirable traits and spotlight red flags.
At the same time, numerous organizations representing the disability community have warned of the potential of the technology to discriminate against and exclude job seekers with disabilities due to superficial variations in how their resumes may appear when contrasted with the general population.
Now, researchers at the University of Washington have identified a fascinating new layer to these exclusionary dynamics by interrogating OpenAI’s ChatGPT on how references to disability influence how it ranks job candidate resumes.
To begin their investigation researchers from UW’s Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering used one of the study authors’ publicly available CVs as a control. The team then modified the control CV to create six variations with each one citing different disability-related credentials ranging from scholarships and awards to memberships on a diversity, equity and inclusion panel or student organization. Running ChatGPT’s GPT-4 model ten times over to rank the modified CVs against the original version for a real-life “student researcher” job listing at a large software company – the results proved both eye-opening and deflating.
In virtually any other sphere, awards and participation in panels should be recognized as a net positive but due to their association with disability in this experiment across 60 trials, ChatGPT only ranked the disability-modified CVs ahead of the control one quarter of the time. This is in spite of the fact that, aside from the disability-related modifications, all other parts of the CV remained identical to the original.
Delving deeper
Of course, the beauty of a large language model like GPT-4 is the capacity for users to engage in human-like back-and-forth conversations with the chat interface and ask it more about how it reached its conclusions. In this experiment, ChatGPT appeared to make several discriminatory suppositions such as that an autism leadership award was likely to have “less emphasis on leadership roles.” It also determined that a candidate with depression had “additional focus on DEI and personal challenges,” which “detract from the core technical and research-oriented aspects of the role” even though no such challenges were explicitly detailed.
Explaining the uneasy relationship between AI algorithms and disability during a recent interview, Ariana Aboulafia the Center for Democracy and Technology’s Policy Counsel for Disability Rights in Technology says, “Algorithms and algorithmic systems are based on pattern recognition and a lot of folks with disabilities exist outside of a pattern.”
She continues, “These algorithmic systems may, to a certain extent, be inherently incompatible with creating an output that's not discriminatory against people with disabilities.”
Commenting on the UW project specifically, the project’s lead author Kate Glazko said, “Ranking resumes with AI is starting to proliferate, yet there’s not much research behind whether it’s safe and effective…. For a disabled job seeker, there’s always this question when you submit a resume of whether you should include disability credentials. I think disabled people consider that even when humans are the reviewers.
“People need to be aware of the system’s biases when using AI for these real-world tasks,” added Glazko.
The human touch
Nevertheless, the UW research did offer a glimmer of hope. The researchers were able to make the disability-related activity-modified CVs rank higher by using GPT-4’s editor function which allows users to add further customizations to the tool. In this instance, they asked GPT-4 to not exhibit ableist bias and to work with disability justice and DEI principles. With this tweak, bias for all but one of the disabilities tested improved with depression being the exception. CVs associated with deafness, blindness, cerebral palsy, autism and the general term “disability" all improved but only three ranked higher than resumes that didn't mention disability. Overall, this system ranked the disability-modified CVs higher than the control CV 37 times out of 60 after GPT-4 was instructed to be more inclusive.
This suggests that awareness amongst recruiters of the limitations of AI and having tools that can be trained and customized on DEI principles can be part of what remains a complex challenge when it comes to enhancing inclusivity in AI.
Another aspect is growing our understanding of this new and emerging area through more specific research as Senior research author and Allen School professor Jennifer Mankhoff explained:
“It is so important that we study and document these biases,” Mankoff said. “We’ve learned a lot from and will hopefully contribute back to a larger conversation — not only regarding disability but also other minoritized identities — around making sure technology is implemented and deployed in ways that are equitable and fair.”
Aboulafia firmly agrees. Emphasizing that, “There’s always questions of multiple marginalization. So, it’s important to recognize that a straight cisgender, white disabled man is unlikely to have the same experiences with systems and technology as a disabled queer woman of color.”
Aboulafia is a huge exponent of codesigning with the disability community for both building out data sets and auditing tools but acknowledges the limitation that each individual with a disability “can only really speak out to their own lived experience.”
“It can be useful to include people with a disability rights or disability justice background,” Aboulafia says.
“There are just as many ways to be disabled as there are people with disabilities and so having a background in disability rights and justice and coming at things from that framework can help a lot with more cross-disability advocacy.”
Despite being unfathomably complex under the hood, generative AI at its front end is becoming more human-like. Maximizing its potential would appear to be, in large part, about asking it the right questions. Building a more disability-inclusive AI future may be less about talking to computers but simply liaising with the right humans at the right time and taking a moment to truly listen to what they have to say.

title: Council Post: AI Meets Agile: Transforming Project Management For The Future
text:
Vamsi Krishna Dhakshinadhi, Chief Technology Officer at GrabAgile Inc.
In today's tech-driven world, staying competitive means adapting quickly and innovating continuously. Agile methodologies have become the foundation of modern project management, emphasizing flexibility and responsiveness. But now, a complementary technology is amplifying these practices: artificial intelligence (AI). When combined, AI and Agile methods create a transformative effect reshaping industries.
Boosting Agile With AI: A New Dynamic
Agile practices emphasize continuous collaboration and frequent delivery of working software. When AI enters the picture, it brings the power to analyze vast amounts of data rapidly, offering insights and predictions that can fine-tune Agile processes even further. For example, AI can analyze customer feedback and project data overnight, providing actionable insights by the time your team starts their day. This means that AI enables not only faster iterations but also more informed decision-making.
Real-World Success Stories: AI Enhancing Agile
Let's delve into some real-life examples where AI and Agile practices have made a significant impact:
Tech Company’s Testing Transformation: A tech firm implemented AI in their software testing phase. By predicting which parts of the code were most likely to have issues, the AI system allowed human testers to focus their efforts more effectively. This approach significantly reduced testing time by 40%, allowing the team to focus on higher-value testing activities, ultimately enhancing the overall quality of their software.
Retail Giant’s Customer Insights: A retail company used AI to monitor real-time customer purchasing behavior, enabling Agile teams to adapt marketing strategies quickly. This allowed their Agile teams to quickly adapt marketing strategies, leading to higher customer engagement and increased sales.
Innovative Tools: The Fusion of AI and Agile
Several AI-powered tools are becoming indispensable for Agile teams:
Jira With Machine Learning
This project management tool uses machine learning to predict project delays and suggest adjustments, helping teams stay on track.
• Tip: Ensure teams regularly update project data and review AI-generated insights in daily stand-ups to maximize effectiveness.
• Suggestion: Use Jira's analytics to identify and proactively address recurring bottlenecks in sprint planning.
• Technique: Integrate Jira with other tools like Slack or Microsoft Teams to streamline communication and quickly act on AI-driven recommendations.
GitHub Copilot
This tool assists developers by suggesting code snippets and entire functions based on patterns learned from millions of coding projects.
• Tip: Encourage developers to use Copilot as a collaborative partner, integrating its suggestions while maintaining rigorous code reviews to ensure quality.
• Suggestion: Pair junior developers with Copilot to accelerate their learning curve and improve their coding skills through AI-suggested best practices.
• Technique: Regularly review and analyze Copilot's code suggestions to refine its settings and improve its alignment with your project's coding standards.
Trello’s Butler
Butler automates repetitive tasks in Trello, such as organizing cards and setting reminders, freeing up team members to focus on more critical tasks.
• Tip: Customize Butler's automation rules to align with team workflows and regularly update these rules based on feedback to enhance productivity.
• Suggestion: Use Butler to create automatic reports and summaries for team meetings, saving time and ensuring all relevant information is easily accessible.
• Technique: Set up Butler to trigger specific actions based on card movements and due dates, ensuring timely task completion and better workflow management.
These tools do more than save time; they enable teams to work smarter and solve problems more creatively. By leveraging the full capabilities of these AI-powered tools, leaders can enhance their teams' efficiency and drive continuous improvement in their Agile processes.
Challenges In Merging AI With Agile
Integrating AI with Agile practices can be complex. There’s often resistance from team members who are unfamiliar with AI or fear it might replace their jobs. Education and transparency are key to overcoming these challenges related to AI integration. Teams should see AI as a complementary tool that enhances their capabilities, not as a substitute for their expertise.
Conducting regular training sessions and offering clear explanations of how AI tools work can help demystify the technology. It is crucial for team members to understand the benefits of AI fully to embrace its value as an integral part of their workflow.
The Future Of AI And Agile
As AI technology continues to advance, its integration with Agile methodologies will become more seamless. We can expect AI to be embedded in every stage of project management, from planning to execution and review. This integration will not only make processes faster but also make them more precise and adaptable.
A Leaders' Role: Maximizing AI And Agile Synergy
Deep involvement is key for leaders aiming to leverage AI and Agile methodologies. Understand the technology by attending workshops, participating in webinars and staying current with trends. Continuous learning is vital for informed decision-making and effective team guidance.
Encourage a learning culture within your team. Support experimentation with new tools and techniques and offer resources like online courses. This promotes innovation and keeps skills sharp.
Facilitate cross-functional collaboration through regular meetings to ensure alignment and full utilization of AI insights across the organization.
Avoid common pitfalls. Don’t over-rely on AI without human oversight; balance AI insights with human judgment. Involve your team in AI tool selection and implementation to avoid resistance and ensure clear, measurable goals to prevent confusion.
Start with pilot programs to test AI integration, allowing for adjustments before a full rollout. Hold regular training sessions to ensure everyone is comfortable with new tools. Develop performance metrics to track effectiveness and make necessary adjustments.
By understanding the technology, fostering a learning culture and promoting collaboration, leaders can effectively integrate AI with Agile methodologies, ensuring these tools are fully leveraged for sustained success.
Conclusion: Embracing The Future
The combination of AI and Agile methodologies offers a powerful approach to project management. This synergy allows businesses to adapt quickly, make informed decisions and innovate continuously. Companies embracing this combination are not just keeping up with change but are leading it.
Integrating AI into Agile practices equips businesses to navigate complex projects more efficiently and effectively, positioning them for sustained success in a dynamic market environment.

title: Council Post: Software Engineering Challenges In The Age Of AI: The Role Of Strong Engineering Leadership
text:
Sriram Panyam is a cloud and SaaS platforms engineering leader. CTO at DagKnows.
Software engineering in the age of artificial intelligence (AI) promises transformative advancements in development processes and team dynamics. However, alongside these opportunities lie unique challenges that can either amplify or alleviate existing issues faced by high-performing teams. Here, I will dive into five key challenges that can be both exacerbated and mitigated by AI, while outlining actionable strategies for engineering leaders to guide their teams toward success.
1. The Velocity-Quality Paradox
High-performing teams pride themselves on rapid development cycles. However, the pressure to maintain velocity can compromise code quality and introduce technical debt. AI-powered tools like code generation and automated testing can further accelerate development but also risk over-reliance on AI and decreased focus on foundational software engineering principles.
To navigate this paradox, engineering leaders should invest in comprehensive training programs for engineers, ensuring they understand AI tool limitations and best practices. Strict code review guidelines must be enforced, emphasizing human scrutiny even for AI-generated code. Additionally, robust monitoring and logging systems can track AI tool performance, identifying biases and errors early on.
2. Scalability And Managing Technical Debt
High-performing teams often grapple with scaling challenges, as projects grow in complexity and technical debt accumulates. Generative AI, by lowering barriers to product development, can exacerbate this issue by accelerating feature creation. This may lead to rushed decisions and suboptimal solutions.
To mitigate this, leaders should encourage a modular, scalable and maintainable architecture from the outset, allowing for easier integration of AI components. AI-powered code analysis tools can identify potential technical debt hotspots, enabling proactive refactoring and maintenance. Leaders should also foster a culture of continuous improvement, encouraging engineers to regularly review and optimize code with a focus on explainability.
3. The Talent War
Top software talent has always been challenging. AI has intensified competition for top talent by creating new categories of specialists (AI engineers, ML experts and data scientists). Second, AI has applications across various industries, not just technology. This broadens the competition for AI talent beyond traditional software companies, attracting talent from sectors like finance, healthcare and manufacturing. Consequently, leaders face fierce competition both within their industry and from entirely new segments. Retaining existing engineers and attracting new AI specialists requires a multifaceted approach.
Leaders should create a culture of innovation and experimentation, offering challenging AI projects to engage engineers. Competitive compensation and benefits packages, including professional development opportunities in AI, are essential.
A supportive and inclusive work environment that values diversity and encourages collaboration further enhances retention. Showcasing the organization's commitment to AI and its potential impact attracts talent passionate about shaping the future of technology.
4. Team Dynamics And Collaboration
AI can both enhance and hinder team dynamics. AI-powered communication tools can streamline collaboration, but over-reliance on AI-driven decision-making can stifle creativity, cause disengagement and affect collaboration.
Leaders should encourage open communication and knowledge sharing, fostering a collaborative environment where team members feel empowered to challenge AI-generated suggestions and contribute their unique perspectives.
Remember, engineers don't just write code. A large part of their role involves collaboration to capture a problem so it can be executed by a machine. Regular team-building activities and opportunities for informal interaction can strengthen interpersonal relationships, enhancing collaboration and creativity.
5. Ethical Considerations And Bias Mitigation
AI in software engineering raises ethical concerns, particularly regarding bias in AI algorithms and decision-making processes. AI-powered tools may inadvertently perpetuate or amplify existing biases in data, leading to discriminatory outcomes. Engineers and scientists have a responsibility to ensure these technologies are safe and built ethically. This is an added pressure beyond the demands of adjusting to an AI-infused engineering world.
Engineering leaders must prioritize ethical AI development and deployment, ensuring that AI systems are designed and trained with diverse and representative data. Regular audits and bias assessments should be conducted to identify and rectify any discriminatory outcomes. Leaders should also educate team members on the potential biases in AI and encourage critical thinking when interpreting AI-generated results.
Leadership Strategies For Success
Engineering leaders now play a larger role in guiding their teams through the AI revolution. Here are some key strategies to ensure success.
• Embrace continuous learning. AI is rapidly evolving, and leaders must foster a culture of continuous learning and adaptation. Encourage engineers to stay updated on the latest AI advancements and provide resources for ongoing learning and development.
• Champion transparency and explainability. AI tools should be transparent and explainable to ensure trust and accountability. Leaders should prioritize the use of AI tools that provide clear explanations for their decisions and outputs.
• Balance automation with human expertise. While AI can automate tasks, human judgment remains crucial for critical decision-making and creative problem-solving. Leaders should strike a balance between automation and human expertise, leveraging AI to augment, not replace, human capabilities.
• Prioritize ethics and responsibility. AI raises ethical concerns regarding bias, fairness and accountability. Leaders must establish ethical guidelines for AI use and ensure AI systems are designed and deployed responsibly.
• Measure and iterate. Continuously measure the impact of AI tools on team performance and morale, identify areas for improvement and iterate on processes and strategies to maximize the benefits of AI.
Looking Ahead
AI presents both challenges and opportunities for high-performing software engineering teams. Any issues must be addressed proactively. In doing so, engineering leaders can empower their teams to modulate the potential impact of AI on velocity, quality, scalability, team dynamics and ethical considerations.
By embracing continuous learning, transparency and ethical AI practices, organizations can fully utilize the transformative power of AI to drive innovation, improve efficiency and sustain a competitive edge for their software engineering teams.

title: With Robust AI Prospects Is IBM A Better Pick Over Merck Stock Within The Dow Index?
text:
We believe that the computing behemoth IBM (NYSE: IBM) is currently a better pick over the pharmaceuticals giant Merck (NYSE: MRK). The decision to invest often comes down to finding the best stocks within the scope of certain characteristics that suit an investment style. In this case, although these companies are from different sectors, they share a similar revenue base of around $61 billion and both are part of the Dow 30 Index. Although Merck has seen a better revenue growth, IBM is more profitable. There is more to the comparison, and in the sections below, we discuss why we think IBM will outperform Merck in the next three years. We compare a slew of factors, such as historical revenue growth, returns, and valuation.
1. Merck Stock Has Outperformed IBM In The Last Three Years
MRK stock has seen strong gains of 65% from levels of $80 in early January 2021 to around $130 now, vs. an increase of about 40% for IBM stock over this period. In comparison, the S&P 500 is up 45% over this roughly three-year period. However, the increase in MRK and IBM has been far from consistent. Returns for MRK stock were -6% in 2021, 45% in 2022, and -2% in 2023. IBM is one of a handful of stocks that have increased their value in each of the last three years, but that still wasn’t enough for it to consistently beat the market. Returns for the stock were 6% in 2021, 5% in 2022, and 16% in 2023. In comparison, returns for the S&P 500 have been 27%, -19%, and 24% over these years, respectively — indicating that both MRK and IBM underperformed the S&P in 2021 and 2023.
In fact, consistently beating the S&P 500 — in good times and bad — has been difficult over recent years for individual stocks; for heavyweights in the Health Care sector including UNH and JNJ, and even for the megacap stars GOOG, TSLA, and MSFT. In contrast, the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, with a collection of 30 stocks, has outperformed the S&P 500 each year over the same period. Why is that? As a group, HQ Portfolio stocks provided better returns with less risk versus the benchmark index; less of a roller-coaster ride, as evident in HQ Portfolio performance metrics.
Given the current uncertain macroeconomic environment with high oil prices and elevated interest rates, could MRK and IBM face a similar situation as they did in 2021 and 2023 and underperform the S&P over the next 12 months — or will they see a strong jump? Although we think both stocks have limited upside, we think IBM will fare better than MRK.
2. Merck’s Revenue Growth Is Better
Merck has seen its revenue rise at an average annual rate of 13.5% from $41.5 billion in 2020 to $60.1 billion in 2023. On the other hand, IBM’s average revenue growth rate of 3.9% from $55.2 billion to $61.9 billion over this period has been comparatively slower.
Merck’s revenue growth has been driven by the success of Keytruda over the recent years. Keytruda has seen its label expand from Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer to Melanoma, Head & Neck, Cervical, Renal, and many more indications, resulting in a stellar 74% surge in sales to $25 billion in 2023, versus $14 billion in 2020. We think Keytruda will peak at around $32 billion in annual sales and decline thereafter with biosimilars entering the market. Currently, Samsung Bioepis, Amgen, Sandoz, and others are working on development of Keytruda’s biosimilars.
Note that Keytruda accounted for 42% of total Merck’s sales in 2023 and its loss of market exclusivity will result in a meaningful decline in sales, and it will be challenging for Merck to bridge this gap. As such, Merck has been looking at inorganic growth, with acquisitions of Acceleron Pharma in 2021, Prometheus Biosciences in 2023, and Harpoon Therapeutics this year.
Other than Keytruda, Merck’s HPV vaccine – Gardasil – has been gaining market share and has seen its sales rise 126% to $8.9 billion in 2023, compared to $3.9 billion in 2020. Similar to Keytruda, Gardasil will also lose market exclusivity in the U.S. in 2028. However, the decline in Gardasil sales is expected to be less profound and hurting for Merck as opposed to Keytruda.
IBM’s revenue growth is being led by its software products, driven by higher sales of Red Hat products and Data & AI solutions. Red Hat, which was acquired in 2019, has been a key growth driver for IBM, given its large portfolio of open-source technology, its hybrid cloud platform, and its large developer community. IBM’s consulting business has also been doing well, despite a tough market for IT spending. Although AI hasn’t really been a big revenue driver for IBM, this trend is expected to change. IBM has been looking to capitalize on the rising demand for AI in the enterprise space. Last year, it introduced Watsonx, its core platform that enables enterprise clients to train, tune, validate, and deploy customized AI models for their businesses. IBM has said that client demand for AI solutions has been accelerating, with its book of business for Watsonx and generative AI seeing strong growth lately. Look at Watsonx Can Help IBM Stock Gain Lost Ground for more details.
3. IBM Is More Profitable
Merck’s operating margin fell from 13.4% in 2020 to 4.9% in 2023, while IBM’s operating margin expanded from 8.4% to 15.2% over this period. However, the 2023 margin decline for Merck can be attributed to a $10 billion charge recorded in Q2’23 for the Prometheus acquisition. IBM has been focused on cutting costs, indicating that it would reduce costs in 2024 by $3 billion, up from its prior estimate of $2 billion via headcount reduction and greater automation. Looking at the last twelve-month period, IBM’s operating margin of 15% fares much better than 8% for Merck.
Looking at financial risk, both companies are comparable. Merck’s 10% debt as a percentage of equity is much lower than 39% for IBM. However, its 5% cash as a percentage of assets is lower than 14% for IBM, implying that Merck has a better debt position, but IBM has more cash cushion.
4. The Net of It All
We see that IBM is more profitable and has more cash cushion, while Merck has seen better revenue growth and has a better debt position. Now, looking at prospects, we believe IBM is the better choice of the two, given its better prospects. We estimate Merck’s Valuation to be $135 per share, close to its current market price of $130. At its current levels, MRK stock is trading at 15x forward expected earnings of $8.59 on a per share and adjusted basis. The 15x figure is slightly higher than the 13x average seen over the past few years, excluding 2023. This is because the 2023 EPS of $1.51 was much lower due to a $17.1 billion R&D charge related to the Prometheus and Imago acquisitions and upfront payments for collaboration agreements with Kelun-Biotech and Daiichi Sankyo.
In comparison, at its current levels of around $174, IBM stock trades at close to 19x expected 2024 earnings of $9.25 per share. This compares with the 15x average P/E multiple for IBM seen over the last three years.
Overall, we think IBM is likely to offer better returns than Merck in the next three years. Although IBM’s growth rates have been lackluster, we think the rise in valuation multiple seems justified, given that IBM is focusing on core areas such as cloud computing, AI, and automation after divesting its legacy business. IBM is also making mid-size acquisitions to bolster its portfolio of higher-margin software products. It’s likely that Merck may continue to see better revenue growth in the near term due to continued market share gains for Keytruda. However, its stock may still see a downward adjustment to its valuation multiple, as investors account for Keytruda’s loss of market exclusivity in 2028.

title: Council Post: Emerging Trends In AI In Biotech
text:
CEO & Founder, Healr Solutions | MIT Senior Lecturer | Corporate, Non-Profit, & Governmental Board Member.
The intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) and biotechnology is revolutionizing the healthcare landscape, offering opportunities for venture capitalists (VCs) to drive innovation and achieve significant returns on investment. This article delves into the key trends in AI in biotech and provides actionable strategies for VCs to navigate this dynamic sector.
As an executive leading biotech research and a founder of a biotech, I've witnessed firsthand the transformative potential of AI in this field. Additionally, my tenure as a researcher at the Robert Langer Lab at MIT, where I focused on drug discovery, and my role teaching bioethics and biotech business at MIT have given me a comprehensive understanding of the sector's intricacies.
It is crucial to explore these developments now because AI is at a pivotal point in its capacity to create new products that can significantly enhance individuals' health and well-being.
Personalized Medicine
Personalized medicine represents a shift from a one-size-fits-all approach to tailored treatments based on individual genetic profiles, lifestyles and environments. AI algorithms are central to this transformation, enabling the analysis of vast data to predict patient responses to treatments, thus enhancing efficacy and reducing adverse effects. Companies at the forefront of AI-driven personalized medicine, such as Tempus and Foundation Medicine, are developing platforms that offer custom cancer therapies, personalized treatment plans for rare diseases, and precision pharmacogenomics.
AI-Driven Drug Discovery
The traditional drug discovery process is time-consuming and costly, often taking over a decade and billions of dollars to bring a new drug to market. AI is streamlining this process by predicting the efficacy and safety of potential compounds with more speed and accuracy. AI models can analyze chemical databases to identify new drug candidates or repurpose existing drugs for new therapeutic uses. Companies leading the trend in drug discovery include Insilco Medicine and Atomwise. This trend is particularly promising for addressing unmet medical needs and accelerating the development of treatments for complex diseases.
Synthetic Biology
Companies are harnessing AI for gene editing, biomaterial production and synthetic pathways are at the forefront of synthetic biology. This combines principles of biology and engineering to design and construct new biological entities. AI optimizes synthetic biology processes, from designing genetic circuits to scaling up production. For example, Ginkgo Bioworks uses AI to design custom microorganisms for applications ranging from pharmaceuticals to industrial chemicals.
Regenerative Medicine
AI is transforming regenerative medicine by advancing the development of stem cell therapies and tissue engineering. AI algorithms assist in identifying optimal cell types, predicting cell behavior and personalized treatments, which is particularly relevant for conditions such as neurodegenerative diseases, heart failure and orthopedic injuries. Organovo, for instance, is leveraging AI to potentially improve the efficacy and scalability of regenerative therapies, developing next-generation treatments that offer the potential to restore function and improve the quality of life for patients.
Data Integration
One of the biggest challenges in healthcare is the integration of disparate data sources, including genomic, proteomic and clinical data. For AI to deliver meaningful insights, seamless data integration and interoperability are critical. Startups developing platforms facilitating comprehensive, longitudinal patient data analysis are vital enablers of AI in biotech. Companies like Flatiron Health are working on integrating diverse datasets to provide a holistic view of patient health, enabling more accurate diagnoses and personalized treatment plans. VCs should prioritize investments in companies that break down data silos and promote data interoperability, as this will enhance the utility and impact of AI-driven solutions.
Strategies For VCs
Focus on clinical validation.
Look at companies that prioritize clinical validation of their AI technologies. Clinical trials and real-world evidence not only enhance credibility but also accelerate market adoption. For example, Novartis’ CAR-T therapy, Kymriah, received the FDA’s accelerated approval for treating relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma, thanks to the integration of real-world evidence (RWE) with clinical trials data from the Phase II ELARA trial. VCs should look for companies with robust clinical trial data and partnerships with leading healthcare institutions. This focus on validation ensures that the technologies being developed are innovative, clinically relevant and ready for deployment in real-world settings.
Foster collaborative ecosystems.
Encourage portfolio companies to build partnerships with academic institutions, healthcare providers and pharmaceutical companies to foster a collaborative ecosystem that accelerates research and development. These partnerships can provide access to valuable resources, including clinical data, research expertise and regulatory insights. For instance, companies like IBM Watson Health have formed strategic alliances with academic medical centers to enhance their AI-driven healthcare solutions. Through this practice, VCs can help their portfolio companies leverage external expertise and resources to advance their technologies and achieve commercial success.
Emphasize ethical AI.
To build trust and mitigate regulatory and public scrutiny risks, companies should prioritize transparency, accountability and fairness in their AI algorithms. This includes addressing patient privacy, data security, and algorithmic bias issues. VCs should seek companies with clear ethical guidelines and robust data governance frameworks. For example, companies like Google Health and Microsoft are known for their commitment to ethical AI practices, which enhances their reputation and market acceptance.
Support scalable solutions.
VCs should focus on companies that develop scalable solutions that can be easily integrated into existing healthcare infrastructures. Scalable innovations ensure broader adoption and maximize return on investment. Digitally transformed incumbents—those leveraging digital technologies to compete innovatively and those venturing into new industries digitally—are twice as likely to achieve outstanding financial growth compared to their traditional counterparts, as shown by a McKinsey study. VCs should assess the scalability potential of AI platforms, considering factors such as compatibility with existing systems, ease of implementation and cost-effectiveness. Companies that offer modular and flexible solutions, such as cloud-based platforms and API integrations, are well-positioned to scale their technologies and achieve widespread market penetration.
Conclusion
The fusion of AI and biotechnology presents a wealth of opportunities for venture capitalists. By staying attuned to emerging trends and adopting strategies for impactful investments, VCs can drive innovation and create transformative changes in healthcare.

title: Council Post: Where CIOs Must Focus To Sustain Generative AI Momentum
text:
Naveen Zutshi is the CIO of Databricks.
Generative AI remains a top investment priority for most organizations. And hopes are high. Among U.S. CEOs, 61% expect AI to change how their business generates value, according to a recent PwC survey. But to get to that point, enterprises have to translate AI hype into reality.
The good news is they’re getting better at doing that. In fact, based on the results of Databricks' recent State of Data + AI report, which breaks down where companies are focusing their efforts, companies moved 1,342% more models from experimentation to the real world. And they’re not slowing down on their data and AI ambitions. The number of experimental models also grew 134%.
These are encouraging signs. But based on my conversations with CIOs and other technical leaders, the challenge is now sustaining that momentum. Companies are struggling to align on expectations. Naturally, many executives want an immediate return on these investments. And amid fear that rivals are moving faster on AI, companies aren't thinking about the long-term strategy.
That’s the wrong approach. Companies that only focus on the “right now” will find themselves jumping from one shiny toy to the next. Generative AI is all about the long game, and CIOs must shift the company’s AI mindset from short-term wins to long-term business transformation. With that in mind, these are the three key areas CIOs and other technical leaders should focus on as they navigate these challenges:
1. Improving Data Infrastructure
Priorities and focus areas for AI are evolving almost as rapidly as the technology itself is.
For example, six months ago, few CIOs were familiar with retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. Now, training commercial LLMs on private company data for better and more tailored performance is a huge focus area. Based on our own anonymized usage data, the use of vector databases, which are key to building RAG models, grew 377% in the past year. Some, like Databricks, are even beginning to use an “agent and tool” approach to help the AI systems solve more complex questions.
This is a testament to how quickly GenAI is advancing, and how fast the breadth of capabilities is expanding alongside that. But data migration remains a challenge. To build a successful RAG system, for example, the data needed to train it must be readily available—not trapped in silos around the organization. Both structured and unstructured data needs to come together to ensure the models can provide the tailored answers that users will expect.
But that is just today’s challenge. Businesses need a framework that can scale as needs and technology changes. Leaders should ask themselves the following: What infrastructure will make it possible to effectively govern, maintain, and glean insights from our data regardless of how the larger AI landscape evolves? What type or size of models excel at the applications are we hoping to use? And how does our data environment need to improve or change to play well with those models?
2. Navigating Foundational Models
For most businesses, general-purpose LLMs are fantastic starting points. And we continue to see increasing usage on our platform. But the more companies use these foundational models, the more they discover the limitations.
It’s why so many are now looking to techniques like RAG and fine-tuning to improve the performance of the model—and ultimately reduce the cost to run it. While companies are doing this work on proprietary models, they’re increasingly opting for open systems. In fact, based on our findings in our report, just a few weeks after Llama 3 was released, it accounted for 39% of all open source model usage.
As these techniques become more ubiquitous, enterprises need to learn when to apply which. For example, organizations may be determined to build their own models from scratch when it may be more cost-effective to just fine-tune a foundational model. Or they may be dealing with constantly updated information sets. In those instances, RAG is a better option because of the speed with which businesses can feed the models new data.
Importantly, models are only getting better. A keen eye toward what’s on the horizon is critical.
Prioritizing Accuracy In The Development And Use Of AI
AI is transforming workflows and reshaping how organizations think about data. But many companies are still in the testing and experimentation phase. That’s because, today, many models aren’t as accurate or reliable as they need to be.
Some companies have already seen the consequences: one airline’s chatbot offered a refund that didn’t fall under the company’s formal policy—and the court ruled with the customer. Or consider a car dealership’s chatbot offering a customer a car for a dollar.
If these missteps occur at scale or in high-stakes scenarios, organizations will suffer. It’s why keeping humans in the loop is vital, especially for applications that require a high degree of accuracy.
And even as models improve, the outputs are only as good as the data supporting them. Strong data hygiene and oversight are key to setting an organization up for AI-driven success. Ensuring that data is governed, accessible and well-architected today will help organizations see more consistently reliable outputs tomorrow.
AI will increasingly be able to augment human capabilities in workplaces across healthcare, manufacturing, enterprise technology and beyond. It’s why businesses need to focus on maintaining strong data infrastructure and practices, prioritizing AI applications that make sense with their broader business strategy and developing an AI-ready workforce that’s ready for this era of change.
