title: ‘Cheap Fake’ Videos Getting Nabbed Via Generative AI
text:
The hottest buzzword or catchphrase right now seems to be “cheap fakes”.
In today’s column, I’ll explain what cheap fakes are, including how they contrast to deepfakes, and share with you some of the ways that generative AI and large language models (LLMs) are aiming to help deal with the rapidly expanding scourge of cheap fakes. For my prior coverage on generative AI and the emergence of deepfakes, see the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Let’s jump right into the matter at hand.
Clarifying What Cheap Fakes Are Versus Deepfakes
The notion of deepfakes is pretty much widely known, while the nature of cheap fakes seems to be a lot less familiar to most people. I’ll start by explaining deepfakes and then launch into the cheap fakes realm.
A deepfake consists of using AI to devise a fake video or the like (e.g., fake picture, fake audio, fake text). I’m sure you’ve seen a deepfake before. A celebrity or a politician might be portrayed via AI to be saying something they didn’t actually say or might be moving around or dancing in a manner that they didn’t actually do. Deepfakes are routinely posted on social media and covered in mainstream news.
In a sense, it is almost ho-hum to deride the rise of deepfakes, simply because the roar of concern and outrage about them has been fervently screaming for a while now. The political arena is especially aflush with deepfakes. People who oppose this or that candidate will readily use AI to craft a deepfake to embarrass or create a scandal associated with the targeted person. The skill level of the person using the AI can be rock bottom because they let the AI do all the heavy lifting and perform for them all the technical intricacies needed to make the deepfake.
Deepfakes are easy-peasy to create due to the advent of advanced AI.
What then is a cheap fake?
A cheap fake is the same kind of fakery as a deepfake, but instead of using AI to craft the untoward content, the adverse content is crafted by the human hand and via so-called non-AI low-tech editing capabilities. A few years ago, we commonly referred to this as “photoshopping” content. You would load a photo of someone into an image-oriented editing package, move around the mouse, and click here and there, altering what the person looked like.
A cheap fake is said to be “cheap” due to not using AI, almost as though you have cut corners and opted to go old-school to devise fake content. You are a cheapskate who doesn’t want to pony up to use modern-day AI in your endeavors of crafting fakeries.
That being said, cheap fakes are a bit more sophisticated these days because we have better editing software. You can edit just about any medium such as a photo, an image, a video clip, an entire video, an audio stream, etc. The process at times is laborious. You might have to go frame-by-frame in a video to make the changes you want to have shown. There is a skill level of a sort that is needed to suitably make use of the features in such editing packages.
The gist overall is that deepfakes and cheap fakes end up with the same end result, namely producing fake, false, or misleading content, and the effort required to produce such content is either done with the assistance of AI in the use case of deepfakes or done without the use of AI in the use case of cheap fakes.
Twists And Turns Enter Into The Big Picture
There are a lot of twists and turns that go into this controversial topic.
One twist is that even though a cheap fake is supposed to be content that is put together without the assistance of AI, the vexing trouble there is that much of the current editing software now includes built-in AI capabilities. Thus, even if you use a vanilla-flavored editing package, the odds are relatively strident that you are tapping into AI during the labored effort to make fake content (i.e., whether you realize or not that the AI is hidden inside the package and doing work for you).
At this moment in time, the cheap fake moniker is being used in a loosey-goosey way.
People who use the catchphrase are kind of looking the other way when it comes to the idea that editing packages contain AI-powered features. The slight escape hatch is that the editing software might not be using generative AI, a particular type of AI. Instead, the editing software uses other AI capabilities having to do with more traditional image processing and video transformation features.
Inch by inch, you can expect that editing software will encompass generative AI. Period, end of story.
In that way of thinking, the catchphrase about cheap fakes will technically have a very short shelf life. Notice that I said it will technically have a brief run. I’m sure that people will continue to use the cheap fake moniker despite the lack of technical aptness. The allure of referring to something as a cheap fake is abundantly strong. It won’t matter to some that they have lost the meaning of the catchphrase. The powerful connotations of dissing something by saying it is a cheap fake will give the naming a longer life than any technical merits sensibly allow.
I have another twist for you.
You might try to hang your hat on the supposition that the number or magnitude of alterations performed by AI is the cornerstone. That’s an added twist to this.
Here’s what I mean.
Someone launches an editing package that contains AI capabilities. They eschew relying on AI by turning off the AI features or avoiding using them. The person mightily attempts to edit content to make it fakery by doing as much by hand as they can. They are still using a computer to aid their efforts. What they have opted to do is avoid the AI being in-the-loop, as much as they can (though probably can’t switch off all the AI capabilities entirely, only the more apparent AI aspects).
If you are willing to say that minimal use of AI is still within the definition of a cheap fake, you could argue that the person indeed created a cheap fake. The problem of course is we are left in a gray area about how much AI they ended up using. Was the AI only 1% of the editing effort, 10%, 50%, 90%, or what portion?
What is the considered allowed cutoff to still stay within the bounds of being a cheap fake?
Some would insist that we are getting stuck arguing fine points and debating how many angels can dance on the head of a pin (an old adage concerning silly or absurd arguments).
Cheap Fakes Are Old And Yet New Again
I hope I’ve garnered your interest in this rather head-scratching catchphrase.
You almost certainly heard the ballyhoo about cheap fakes in the last week or so, having become a storm in the political presidential race.
Here’s the convoluted morass.
If you accuse a fake video of being a deepfake, but if it wasn’t crafted via the use of AI, someone else who wants to attack your attack of that fake video will insist that it isn’t a deepfake and that you lied when claiming it was. Your lie isn’t regarding the video being faked; it is instead a said-to-be lie about it being devised with the use of AI and ergo not being a deepfake per se.
Do you see the subtly there?
Your best bet, assuming that you don’t know for sure that the fake was devised via the use of AI, would be to refer to the fake video as a cheap fake. Someone else will have to essentially prove that it was devised via the help of AI in order to now call you a liar. At this time, since there isn’t as much obvious AI embedded into editing software, the burden of proof of the attacker has been raised for now (later, such as a year from now, the burden will shift to the other side).
Saying that something is a cheap fake gets you onto safer ground in comparison to saying that it is a deepfake.
There are other advantages too of switching to using the cheap fake moniker.
We are all now somewhat worn out about calls of things being deepfakes. It doesn’t register with us anymore as something out of the ordinary. The claim is used nonstop. Our ears are numb to the wording.
The phrase of something being a cheap fake is a wake-up call. Few realize that cheap fakes as a moniker have been around for several years. Many think the cheap fake notion was just invented or discovered in the last few weeks. It seems utterly new to them.
The reality is that cheap fakes are old hat.
There is a sensible reason for this.
Allow me to explain.
Around 2018 and 2019, the idea of referring to a faked photo or video was starting to stand out. Few editing software packages had much if any AI built in. You had to go to a separate AI component or package to do AI-related work. The demarcation then between deepfakes and cheap fakes was a lot clearer.
It made notable sense to refer to some items as cheap fakes and others as deep fakes. The use of the traditional editing packages that lacked AI was what constituted cheap fakes. The use of specialized AI packages that could be used to generate fakeries was reserved for the deepfakes moniker.
Life was simpler at that time.
Since then, the world has blurred because AI has been infused into all manner of packages, including editing software.
We are clinging to the old days of sharp demarcation between cheap fakes and deepfakes, yet we are in a modern world where the distinction is gradually shrinking and will soon enough disappear. Probably, the only way to genuinely create a cheap fake will be to reload an old version of an editing package, one that existed before modern times, or maybe resort to true by-hand efforts such as trick photography, though that seems an unlikely ongoing scenario.
Or we might all agree to a new definition for cheap fakes. That’s always another option. Just change the meaning to fit whatever notions we want it to mean. Words are malleable in that fashion.
Claims About Cheap Fakes Can Be Real Or Fake
Tighten your seatbelt because I’ve got additional mind-benders in store for you.
Suppose that someone says that a particular video is a cheap fake.
Are they right or wrong?
Well, they could be “wrong” in the sense that it is a deepfake, and not a cheap fake. I covered that a moment ago.
They could also be wrong if it turns out that the video is completely unaltered and not touched up beyond whatever the original video consisted of. In other words, if the notion of a fake is that it is dependent upon a true original, you could presumably merely get a true copy of the original, compare it to the claimed-to-be cheap fake, and see if they match.
Any mismatches might be attributed to someone messing around with the claimed fake, and you then are on the high ground to say it is a fake. Meanwhile, if the true original and the claimed fake are identical, you would seem to be on quicksand as to claim that the other video is a fakery. The other video is presumably a carbon copy, as it were, matching precisely to the original video. No fuss, no muss.
Unfortunately, the world is never that straightforward.
For example, would even the tiniest of edits constitute that the second video is a fake? You can debate this. There might be minor differences between one video and the seemingly same video, such that offensively smearing the second video as an outright fake is going overboard. You are nearly yelling wolf when there is not a wolf in the woods. We might be willing to allow for minor variations as long as the majority of what is there still shows the same gist of things.
Of course, in a politically charged hotbed, the leveraging of the slightest of differences is bound to be readily made use of. You don’t have to claim that something is fake when there is only a substantive difference. You can appear to be completely aboveboard by finding a teensy weeny difference and making a mountain out of a molehill. That’s the way the ball bounces in politics.
The other video that is smeared by the claim of being a cheap fake now has to dig its way out of a hole. Everyone will presumably take at face value that the claim of a cheap fake is being made on a bona fide basis. The burden becomes trying to resurrect the reputation of the smeared video. It might be a hurdle that cannot be overcome, no matter how hard you try.
Quite a conundrum.
Another factor to consider is that cheap fakes are often defined as consisting of two somewhat distinct fakery-related facets: (1) editing, and (2) out-of-context (OCC).
A cheap fake video might be an edited version of an original video. Someone let’s say uploaded an original video, changed the video to make a person in the video look like they are frozen rather than in motion, and then released the newly edited video into the public sphere. In this instance, two videos are floating around. There is the original unedited video, and we now have an edited version that could be construed as a cheap fake.
That’s what we usually have happen.
A different approach to a cheap fake involves trying to impact the context of the video. Suppose that we upload a video, and it is a minute in length. A person in the video is midway through the video reaching out their hand to shake another person’s hand. The other person’s hand doesn’t come into the frame until the 41st second time slot after the first person extends their hand. To make it look like the first person is handshaking to a ghost, we lop off the portion where the second person enters the frame. The resulting 40-second video is still the same as the original, but we have lopped off the remaining 20 seconds.
Do you see how this is a fakery associated with being out-of-context?
The viewer of the shortened clip is not going to be aware that a second person is standing there and ready to shake hands with the first person. You would almost easily fall for the idea that the first person is seeking to shake the hand with nothing other than thin air. Only when you see the longer and full video would you realize that a second person existed and was going to be shaking the first person’s hand.
An out-of-context video can be just as impactful as an edited video.
I have a quick question for you. Would you say that the act of clipping the video is a form of editing, or would you say that since the act is only lopping off a segment of video this isn’t an edit per se? Some would exhort that the shortening of the video is, in fact, a form of editing. Thus, the video has been edited. Others would claim that there weren’t any edits made. The video was merely shortened in length.
I assume you can see that a lot of political fodder can be used on either side of that coin.
The Slippery Slope Of Making Fakery Claims
There are additional ways of formulating an out-of-context formulation that more definitively lands in the editing sphere. I take a video and force a portion of the video to zoom in. When you watch the newly reformulated video, you see a close-up of the person’s hands. The hands aren’t edited, only the aspect that you can abundantly see the hands, which are now front-and-center. They were less obvious to the eye in the original video.
It could be persuasively argued that this is a form of editing, namely that you used a zoom feature and edited the video. In contrast, the earlier lopping off a portion of the video smells less like an outright edit. You be the judge of where the dividing line resides of what is an edit versus not an edit. The dividing line is open to heated debate.
A cheap fake might consist of these formulations: (a) edited alterations, (b) an out-of-context reconstitution, or (c) a combination that mixes the use of editing and out-of-context instantiations.
All in all, we ought to consider seven key uses of or claims about cheap fakes:
- (1) Legitimate claim that something is a cheap fake as per having been edited (substantiveness comes into question).
- (2) Legitimate claim that something is a cheap fake as per being rendered out-of-context (substantiveness comes into question).
- (3) Legitimate claim that something is a cheap fake that mixes edits and out-of-context (substantiveness comes into question).
- (4) Legitimate claim that something is a deepfake rather than a cheap fake (the AI usage question is narrowing this gap).
- (5) False claim that something is a cheap fake when it is instead a deepfake.
- (6) False claim that something is a deepfake when it is a cheap fake.
- (7) False claim that something is a cheap fake when it is precisely the same as the original in all respects and does not merit the cheap fake clamor.
I bring those various possibilities to your attention because there is a chance that a claim about something being a cheap fake or even a deepfake is ostensibly incorrect. The person making such a claim might do so without any evidence to support their claim. It is a handy dandy means of smearing a video, photo, or any item that though a true version, doesn’t portray what is desired or preferred.
The person making the smear can also buy themselves some plausible deniability by saying that they believe or assume that this or that is a cheap fake or a deep fake. In that way of conveying the smear, they buy themselves room to maneuver. First, they don’t need to provide proof of their claim. Second, if later it is proven that the item is not a cheap fake or a deepfake, and that it is genuine, the person can shrug their shoulders and note that they simply thought it might be a fakery. You can’t seemingly hold them accountable for what seemed to be a fake. They didn’t say for absolute certainty it was a fake.
Our world is murky and the same applies to claims associated with cheap fakes and deepfakes.
Those who wish to use the labeling to their advantage can do so. This in turn confounds situations involving actual cheap fakes and deepfakes. It is challenging to know whether something is a cheap fake or not. Those who have a legitimate claim are at times frustrated and exasperated by other false claims that make their true claims seem false.
As you can clearly see, this is not as much of an exact science as others often lead us to believe.
What To Do About The Increasing Glut Of Cheap Fakes
Deepfakes and cheap fakes are a growing industry.
This makes a lot of sense. Disinformation and misinformation are increasingly afoot. Deepfakes and cheap fakes are a form of disinformation and misinformation. Our information-based society that relies on social media and digital interactions will be rampant with deepfakes and cheap fakes. It all goes hand-in-hand.
At first, the labor and skills required to make cheap fakes were something that kept the abundance of cheap fakes partially in check. Meanwhile, the deepfakes made use of AI, and assuming you could afford the cost of using AI, the ease of producing deepfakes in volume was like falling off a log. Automation came to your aid.
I mentioned earlier that it is going to be easier to make cheap fakes due to the infusion of AI into conventional editing software. The bottom line is that making cheap fakes is also going to be as easy as falling off a log. Whether you like that or not, it is a new reality.
How are we going to cope with an abundance of cheap fakes?
In prior columns, I’ve discussed how the use of generative AI is being devised to either prevent people from creating deepfakes and/or being used to detect deepfakes, the link here and the link here.
Let’s focus here on the use of generative AI to detect cheap fakes. The thinking is that if we can use AI to ferret out cheap fakes, doing so will allow us to use automation to forewarn when a cheap fake is upon us. Furthermore, we can use AI to help in sorting out legitimate claims versus false claims of cheap fakes being in hand.
To give you a heads-up, there is no silver bullet to be had via AI.
Do not put your hopes and dreams on AI solving this dilemma. In some useful ways, generative AI is going to be helpful. Lamentedly, in other ways, generative AI is going to be unhelpful.
For example, I’ve written extensively about the downsides of AI detectors that try to identify whether a student paper was written by AI or made by the hands of a student, see the link here and the link here. There are many false positives and false negatives in these endeavors, and at times students who put their heart and soul into writing an essay are egregiously and unfairly being reputationally maligned. This is either due to unreliable AI detectors or by people who use AI detectors and don’t comprehend the limitations and false detections being made. It’s a mess. It is at times a total travesty.
I’d suggest that when it comes to detecting cheap fakes, there is a long road yet to go and that along the way we need to keep our wits about us and not let the emergence of AI-based tools that claim to be “surefire cheap fake” detectors do a snow job on society.
Okay, I will get down from the soap box, sorry, had to say this since it is vitally important.
On with the show.
In the AI field, there is an ongoing grand challenge associated with finding ways to devise AI that will detect cheap fakes. A research article posted in 2021 entitled “MMSys’21 Grand Challenge on Detecting Cheap Fakes” by Shivangi Aneja, Cise Midoglu, Duc-Tien Dang-Nguyen, Michael Alexander Riegler, Pål Halvorsen, Matthias Nießner, Balu Adsumilli, and Chris Bregler, axXiv, July 12, 2021, made these points (excerpts):
- “Cheap fake is a recently coined term that encompasses non-AI (‘cheap’) manipulations of multimedia content.”
- “Cheap fake media can be created using editing software for image/video manipulations, or even without using any software, by simply altering the context of an image/video by sharing the media alongside misleading claims.”
- “Depending on the type of cheap fake media, different detection tools need to be developed.
- “For instance, methods to detect image manipulations such as photoshopping and image splicing have been investigated. Re-contextualization or out-of-context (OOC) misuse, which includes associating falsified or unrelated claims with a genuine image in order to misrepresent events or persons is, however, relatively niche and unexplored.”
Please note that as mentioned, the above was from 2021, some three years ago, and thus reinforcing my point that cheap fakes as a moniker were not born yesterday.
In a more recent study that occurred last year, a study entitled “Cheap-fake Detection With LLM Using Prompt Engineering” by Guangyang Wu, Weijie Wu, Xiaohong Liu, Kele Xu, Tianjiao Wan, and Wenyi Wang, arXiv, June 5, 2023, the research paper made these salient points (excerpts):
- “On social media, two principal forms of deceptive information regularly encountered are deepfakes and cheap fakes.”
- “While ‘deepfakes’ refer to videos that have been doctored using machine learning or other AI-based methods to create or combine human faces and bodies, ‘cheap fakes’ are a far less costly variant of doctored videos generated through readily available software tools such as Photoshop, Premiere Pro, among others.”
- “Cheap fakes are often created through manipulating image captions, image editing or by adjusting video speed. Due to their ease of creation, cheap fakes are perceived to be more ubiquitous and damaging than deepfakes.”
And we can reach back to 2019, noting a report entitled “Deepfakes And Cheap Fakes” by Britt Paris and Joan Donovan, Data & Society, September 18, 2019, making these points about cheap fakes (excerpts):
- “Deepfakes which rely on experimental machine learning represent one end of a spectrum of audiovisual AV manipulation.”
- “Other forms of AV manipulation – ‘cheap fakes’ – rely on cheap, accessible software, or no software at all.”
- “Both deepfakes and cheap fakes are capable of blurring the line between expression and evidence.”
- “Society is already struggling to mitigate the harm of ‘traditional’ techniques: changes in speed, cutting apart or together, circulating in new, vulnerable contexts. It is into this landscape that so-called deepfakes emerge.”
- “Visual evidence is not only interpreted in formal courtroom settings. Within journalism, visual evidence plays a key role in the construction of public opinion and the arrangement of political power.”
You might have noticed in that last point above an indication about courtroom settings.
The issue of cheap fakes and deepfakes is a huge one when it comes to trials and our justice system, see my coverage at the link here and the link here. It is one thing to have a cheap fake or deepfake that smears someone in the public sphere, but having a cheap fake or a deepfake that could potentially be used in a criminal trial and lead to convicting someone of a crime is a whole different ballgame. There is a great deal of focus on the use of digital forensics techniques and technology to ferret out whether a photo, image, audio recording or video is fair game for submission as evidence. This is serious stuff.
Diving Into The Details Of Generative AI For Cheap Fake Detection
In the case of detecting deepfakes, it is said that you can fight fire with fire. This means that since deepfakes rely upon AI to craft the deepfake, we might as well try using AI to detect those deepfakes. Fighting AI with AI.
We are (arguably) agreeing that cheap fakes don’t make use of AI, thus, you can’t presumably refer to using AI to catch cheap fakes as using AI to catch AI. The idea is that we are using AI to catch the trickery of humans who are seeking to make cheap fakes. I would take that depiction with a grain of salt. Recall that I’ve noted that increasingly AI will be used in the process of composing cheap fakes, regardless of whether a user realizes that AI is taking a role in the cheap fake act or not.
How can AI, and especially generative AI, be used to detect cheap fakes?
I’m glad you ask, thanks.
A simple approach would be to enter a prompt into generative AI and ask that the AI tell you whether a particular video or audio that you load into the generative AI is a cheap fake. Right now, the odds of the AI doing an adequate job on this is somewhat low. The advent of multi-modal generative AI is still just getting underway. Text-oriented analyses are generally more so in the bailiwick at this time rather than analyses of images or video for fakery.
I opted to try out ChatGPT to see how a generic generative AI might do in ferreting out cheap fakes. I say generic generative AI because there are specialized AI-based forensic apps that are designed for doing these kinds of detections. They are honed for that specific purpose.
The answer I got from ChatGPT noted these ways that generative AI can potentially attempt to detect cheap fakes (excerpts from my chat with ChatGPT GPT-4o):
- “Image and Video Analysis: AI models can analyze the consistency of images and videos. Generative AI, trained on large datasets, can identify discrepancies such as unnatural shadows, inconsistent lighting, or irregularities in the pixel structure that might indicate manipulation.”
- “Contextual Verification: AI can cross-reference the content with known authentic sources. For example, it can check the time and location metadata against a database of verified images or videos to see if the content has been misrepresented or shown out of context.”
- “Audio Analysis: AI can detect unnatural modifications in audio files. It can identify changes in pitch, speed, and other acoustic features that might indicate the audio has been tampered with.”
- “Text Analysis: For text-based cheap fakes, AI can analyze linguistic patterns and cross-check facts against reliable sources. It can also detect inconsistencies in the narrative or style that suggest the content has been manipulated.”
- “Deep Learning Models: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) and other deep learning models can be trained to recognize the subtle artifacts left behind by simple editing techniques. These models can compare the suspicious content to a vast array of genuine content to spot anomalies.”
- “Forensic Tools: AI-based forensic tools can examine the metadata of digital files, looking for signs of editing or manipulation. These tools can often identify when and how a file was altered, providing evidence of a cheap fake.”
Those are on-target points.
You’ll note that the higher likely chance entails having the original referent video or audio to make a comparison to. This makes the task a straight-ahead comparison. The main issue is that other than determining that essentially bit-for-bit they are the same, ergo the second one is not presumably cheap fake in that case, you must make some judgments about any differences that might arise.
For example, we could opt to alter the format of a video and have a different video on a purely bitwise basis. A human who watches the video might not see any visually discernable difference between the original and the alleged cheap fake. Is the alleged cheap fake an actual cheap fake or can we overlook the fact that the format differs?
If you don’t have access to an original referent, the task gets complicated. I gave an example earlier of lopping off the remainder of a video that showed a person shaking the hand of another person. Suppose you only had 40 seconds worth of video. Suppose you didn’t know there was any additional video involved. It would be problematic to say that the video was a cheap fake.
One insider aspect is that depending upon the format of the video, there often is a hidden-from-view portion that describes facets of the video, customarily referred to as the metadata. The metadata for a one-minute video might indicate that the video is one minute in length. If someone lops off the last 20 seconds and doesn’t alter the metadata, there is a chance that the metadata will still say that the video is supposedly a minute in length. You could look at the metadata to try and see if it squares with what you have in hand. The issue here is that the metadata is usually easily altered and anyone who knows what they are doing would likely double-check to ensure that the metadata matches the now altered video.
This brings up an important point overall.
There is a continual cat-and-mouse gambit between those who make cheap fakes and those who seek to detect cheap fakes. It goes like this. A person makes a cheap fake and tries doing so with all the nuances and tricks they have up their sleeves. The cheap fake is hard to detect. Soon, the detection capabilities will improve, and those cheap fakes will become easier to spot. Lo and behold, the maker of cheap fakes ups their game and does new trickery to avoid those newer forms of detection. And so on this goes. Rinse and repeat, as they say.
I asked ChatGPT to provide a list of the ways that people can devise cheap fakes and aim to avoid detection.
Before I show you the response, I want to mention something about this. Some people think no one should ever reveal the tricks used to make cheap fakes. Their qualm is that doing so helps those who want to make cheap fakes. The posture is that it is better to keep them in the dark.
Though this is a laudable notion, the issue is that one way or another the cheap fake makers will find out about these tricks. Trying to hide it from them is just not practical. In the end, it is better to share the nature of the cheap fake trickery so that we can all see it in the light of day and pursue means to undercut or at least detect when the trickery or fakery is being utilized.
To clarify, there is a degree to which this rule of thumb goes. I wouldn’t advocate making known on a cookie-cutter basis the fakery techniques. That’s almost laying out the meal on a silver platter. As you will momentarily see, usually referring to the fakery methods can be done at a 30,000-foot level which is sufficient to comprehend what’s taking place.
ChatGPT provided me with a list of these eight common cheap fake approaches (excerpts):
- “High-Quality Editing: Using advanced editing tools and techniques to create more seamless alterations. Skilled editors can pay attention to details like lighting, shadows, and textures to make the manipulation less detectable.”
- “Contextual Sophistication: Carefully selecting and altering content to ensure that the context remains plausible. This involves making subtle changes that are less likely to raise suspicion.”
- “Mimicking Genuine Patterns: Analyzing genuine content to understand common patterns and characteristics, then replicating these in the fake content. This includes matching linguistic styles, visual artifacts, and acoustic features.”
- “Layered Manipulation: Combining multiple small edits instead of making a single, obvious alteration. This can include slight adjustments in various parts of an image or video that collectively convey a different message without obvious signs of tampering.”
- “Metadata Manipulation: Altering the metadata of digital files to hide evidence of editing. This can include changing timestamps, GPS data, and other metadata fields to make the content appear authentic.”
- “Using Real Data: Incorporating genuine, unaltered data into the fake content to lend it credibility. For example, using real video footage but altering the audio or vice versa.”
- “Distraction Techniques: Introducing irrelevant but plausible details that draw attention away from the manipulated parts of the content. This can make it harder for AI to focus on the alterations.”
- “Testing Against Detection Tools: Continuously testing the fake content against available detection tools and refining it to avoid detection. This involves understanding the limitations of generative AI and exploiting those weaknesses.”
That last point in the list exemplifies my comment that a cat-and-mouse gambit is always underway.
Not only does a cheap fake maker think ahead about how a detector might try to figure out the cheap fake is a cheap fake, but they can also go ahead and use the cheap fake detection tools to do some testing privately for them. They run and run their cheap fake through a series of detection tools, and each time successively refine their cheap fake so that it hopefully slips under the radar.
Throwing In The Towel Or Remaining Ever Vigilant
I realize that the cat-and-mouse conundrum is somewhat depressing.
Are we always going to have unfettered cheap fakes?
In one sense, yes, the game is going to last a long time. Sad face. I don’t want that to seem pessimistic. The chances are that the side of detecting the cheap fakes will get better faster than the aim to make the cheap fakes. Happy face.
I asked ChatGPT to provide a list of the ways that we can try to combat cheap fakes (excerpts):
- “Advancements in Detection Technology: Continuous improvements in AI and machine learning can enhance our ability to detect fake content. Developing more sophisticated algorithms and tools will make it harder for fake content to go undetected.”
- “Education and Awareness: Raising public awareness about the existence and tactics of fake content can help people become more critical consumers of information. Media literacy programs can teach individuals how to identify and verify authentic content.”
- “Regulation and Policy: Governments and organizations can implement regulations and policies that discourage the creation and dissemination of fake content. This might include legal repercussions for creating or sharing malicious fakes and standards for verifying the authenticity of digital media.”
- “Collaboration Between Platforms: Social media and content-sharing platforms can collaborate to identify and remove fake content more effectively. Sharing data and detection techniques can create a more unified front against misinformation.”
- “Authentication Technologies: Developing and adopting technologies that verify the authenticity of digital content, such as digital watermarks, blockchain, and cryptographic signatures, can help ensure the integrity of information.”
- “Human Oversight: Combining AI with human oversight can improve detection rates. Human experts can provide context and judgment that AI might miss, ensuring a more thorough verification process.”
- “Incentivizing Truth: Creating incentives for producing and sharing verified, truthful content can help shift the focus away from fake content. This could involve promoting verified accounts, providing monetary rewards for debunking fakes, or highlighting trustworthy sources.”
The list goes far beyond the purely technical underpinnings of cheap fakes.
Yes, indeed, we need to think about this issue from a holistic perspective. Technical aspects are a crucial element, certainly. There are societal and other angles to be given due diligence too.
One of those points above indicates that we can try to outlaw the devising of cheap fakes. The idea is that even if people are capable of making cheap fakes and suppose there is no ready way to stop them from doing so, they would run the risk of breaking the law. Perhaps a looming criminal prosecution would make them think twice.
I’ve covered extensively the legal side of these matters, see for example the link here and the link here. One of the counterbalancing impacts of enacting such laws is that it is extremely hard to pin down the legal nuances that on the one hand catch malicious cheap fakes yet don’t crush efforts to be innovative. In addition, another worry is that innocent users will suddenly become tainted as possible criminals, for which the use of such a law could be like using an elephant gun to go after an ant.
Conclusion
A few final comments for now.
Abraham Lincoln purportedly said these immortal words: “You can fool all the people some of the time and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time.”
The issue we have today is that the use of cheap fakes and the rapid dispersion of them via social media can readily fool some of the people for some of the time. We must do our darnedest to ensure that cheap fakes cannot fool all the people all the time. Plus, we need to minimize the fooling of people and reduce the time during which they get fooled.
There is definitely tomfoolery involved in cheap fakes.
The tomfoolery should not be taken lightly. Cheap fakes might very well sway people in society and cause monumental consequences accordingly. The same goes for making false claims about something being a cheap fake when it is a genuine deal. That too is a form of fooling the people.
I’ll give the final word here to Abraham Lincoln: “America will never be destroyed from the outside. If we falter and lose our freedoms, it will be because we destroyed ourselves.”

AI startup Etched raises $120 million to develop specialized chip
Etched said backers in the funding round include former PayPal CEO Peter Thiel and Replit CEO Amjad Masad.
Artificial intelligence (AI) startup Etched said on Tuesday it has raised $120 million in a series-A funding round that the company plans to use to further develop its specialised chip.
The San Francisco-based company aims to make a specialised processor tuned to run a specific kind of AI model that is widely used by OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google Gemini.
Nvidia dominates the market for server AI chips, capturing roughly 80% of sales, according to estimates. Nvidia's general-purpose AI chips are capable of handling a range of computing applications, but can use more energy than processors designed to perform specific functions. Nvidia is the largest U.S. company by market value.
Etched said backers in the funding round include former PayPal CEO Peter Thiel and Replit CEO Amjad Masad.
Engineers at Etched are designing the chip to power the portion of AI computing that generates content and responses, called inference. The chip, which is the first designed by the company, would be optimized to run a specific form of AI model known as a transformer.
"This company is a little bit of a bet," CEO Gavin Uberti said in an interview. "If transformers go away, our company will die. But if they stick around, we're going to be one of the biggest companies of all time."
Etched has partnered with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. to fabricate the chips. Uberti said the company needs the series-A funding to defray the costs of sending its designs to TSMC and manufacturing the chips, a process known as "taping out" a chip.
The company did not disclose its valuation. At the time of its $5.4-million seed-funding round, March 2023, investors valued the business at $34 million.
The 35-person company was founded by Uberti and Chris Zhu.

title: The Shape Of The Composable Enterprise
text:
Business is composable. Spoiler alert, it has actually always been that way i.e. an organization of any form is a generally coalesced gathering of physical resources, intellectual property, processes and people all brought together to form a whole that is greater than the sum of the parts. Since biblical times (let’s imagine a bakery perhaps), organizations have been composable units with specialised skills or at least designated responsibilities.
This age-old truism hasn’t stopped the technology industry from latching onto the term composability for some years now.
Ex-CEO of Red Hat Jim Whitehurst used the term as his keynote address theme somewhere around 2010. Predating the arrival of cloud computing’s orchestration boom in the era of Kubernetes today, Whitehurst had perhaps already sniffed the forthcoming release of his firm’s containerization products and knew that we were about to start talking about technology building blocks with new force.
The Age Of Composability
As we enter the next era of composable computing, the IT trade is keen to amplify the notion of the composable business. But why?
This is because we’re in the age of application programming interfaces where API connectivity gives us maps inside our taxi apps and currency calculators inside our travel booking apps. It’s also because we’re living in a technology period when web-scale integration is possible as we bring together the power of large language models to drive the new tier of generative artificial intelligence that seems to underpin every technology initiative on the planet. Plus, we’re now in a period where work isn’t work as such; we now prefer to talk about workflows, which are made up of jobs, roles, tasks and functions… all of which are now brought together and composed with a higher degree of composability.
Enterprise integration, automation and API management company MuleSoft (part of the Salesforce family) thinks it has a special part to play in the business composability orchestra. Now aiming to elevate its view on the application of automation tools, the company says that the benefits of AI agents needs to happen inside the natural flow of work, not as a separate, siloed process.
“Organizations need a platform designed to build composable architectures — helping them scale and flex as technologies and standards evolve using a diverse set of integration, automation and API management capabilities. Individual building blocks can be used to build more intricate systems and applications in a technology stack, empowering organizations to rapidly adopt new standards and technologies because it is inherently flexible,” said Param Kahlon, Salesforce EVP and GM of automation and integration. “AI-powered composability is MuleSoft’s solution to help organizations build a foundation for the new AI era.”
A Composable Example
To provide an illustrative example of this process in motion, Kahlon asks us to imagine the way connected (not necessarily autonomous) vehicles are being developed today. We already know that drivers today expect more than just four wheels and steering wheel, they expect onboard map navigation, AI-powered safety functions (beeps if a driver takes their hand off the wheel and further alerts to signify the proximity of other traffic and so on) and insight into car performance.
To collect telemetry data, such as driving behavior or the state of the engine, a car manufacturer can compose and integrate their systems using an API-led methodology. He says that once the foundation is set in this vehicle example, AI-powered composability comes in. The automotive company can build reusable building blocks supplied through APIs, integrations, or AI-powered automation flows and integrate LLMs into their architecture.
MuleSoft’s product portfolio that works at this level includes Anypoint Platform, for integration and API management, robotic process automation, intelligent document processing, Composer (technology that integrates both applications and data), plus Salesforce Flow for business process automation. With Salesforce’s AI-engine Einstein, the company says it has built AI into its tools for developers and business teams to integrate and automate faster.
Kahlon insists that the processes connecting and composing with LLM APIs need security and governance just like any other API. It has customers using its API gateways (Anypoint Flex Gateway and Mule Gateway) as LLM gateways with custom-made policies to help them secure and manage their APIs.
What Is An API Gateway?
For completeness and clarity here (and for those with an interest), an API gateway is designed to work as a centralized software tool to manage API activity with traffic management rules, connection protocols and security stipulations. Capable of directing APIs that glue together backend services with frontend applications and services, an API gateway can also help deliver tiered consumption controls so that API consumers can decide which APIs they connect to based on their price, functionality or other characteristics.
“With an API gateway in use, financial institutions can ensure that data stays within their trusted boundaries by developing a custom policy that checks for sensitive customer information before data is shared with a third-party LLM,” said Kahlon. “MuleSoft also has built-in governance rulesets that provide automated conformance checks to help support industry-specific and corporate compliance. For example, banks can include a standard procedure for managing LLM APIs to ensure proper user authentication before gaining access to generative AI capabilities.”
In other words, these are the moving controllable parts of a composable enterprise.
Composable AI
As we now set AI assistants to work inside the composable enterprise, we perhaps need to realize that to be meaningful, AI assistants need to go beyond just executing a search or answering questions.
“They [AI assistants] need to take action with conversational prompts such as updating an employee record or vacation request, creating an order, or updating a customer’s bill. If implemented correctly, AI should take on the repetitive, mundane tasks that humans do currently,” concluded Kahlon. “MuleSoft technology is helping bring these capabilities to life in Einstein Copilot, Salesforce’s predictive and generative AI assistant. Using APIs and integrations built with MuleSoft Anypoint Platform and Salesforce Flow, Copilot can extend its capabilities to leverage data from third-party systems.”
If composability really does encompass the shape of enterprise operational systems in the years ahead (and it arguably will), then it will reflect the deeper trend seen in enterprise software development at large i.e. as our applications, data services and toolsets evolve out of their adolescence, they can become more specialized, more custom-aligned and more finely tuned their required task.
That reality means we have the opportunity to use repeatable blocks of IT for repeatable common tasks across different businesses - and, it means we can use smaller refined pieces of technology to provide the toppings and treats that we need in our services and on our screens. Someone just needs to be there to integrate it all.

title: Author Post: 6 Strategies to Improve Trust in Generative AI in Healthcare
text:
In Deloitte’s latest report, Building and Maintaining Health Care Consumers’ Trust in Generative AI, the findings underscore the critical importance of trust in harnessing the transformative potential of generative AI (gen AI) in healthcare.
Despite high consumer optimism, the adoption of gen AI in healthcare remains stagnant, with trust issues presenting a significant barrier.
The survey, conducted in March 2024 with over 2,000 US adults, highlights several key takeaways. Consumers who have used gen AI for health reasons believe it could reduce appointment wait times and lower individual care costs, with 66% expressing this view. However, overall adoption has regressed to 37% of consumers utilizing it in 2024, compared to 40% in 2023.
Distrust in gen AI-provided information has grown, with 30% of consumers citing it as a reason for non-use in 2024, up from 23% in 2023. This distrust is notably higher among millennials (30% in 2024 vs. 21% in 2023) and baby boomers (32% in 2024 vs. 24% in 2023).
That said, 74% of respondents view doctors as their most trusted source of health information, and consumers are generally comfortable with doctors using gen AI for treatment information (71%), diagnostic interpretation (65%), and diagnosis (53%).
Emerging trends show that while consumer optimism about gen AI’s potential to improve access and affordability persists, adoption rates remain flat due to increasing distrust. Consumers heavily rely on clinician guidance for health decisions involving gen AI.
Key challenges include handling highly sensitive personal data, ensuring AI outputs are accurate and reliable, navigating complex regulations related to patient privacy, data security, and ethical considerations, addressing consumer concerns about data privacy and security, and providing clear information about how gen AI is used in healthcare decisions.
Six Essential Strategies for Building Trust
1. Transparency and Education
Healthcare providers should be transparent about how generative AI is used in patient care, explaining specific use cases, benefits, and limitations. According to Deloitte, 80% of consumers want to be informed about how their healthcare provider uses generative AI to influence care decisions and identify treatment options.
Bill Fera, head of AI at Deloitte, emphasized the importance of transparency, stating, “Hospitals should educate their patients about how and why generative AI is being used at their organization.”
Educational programs can help patients and providers understand the capabilities and limitations of generative AI, alleviating fears and misconceptions through workshops, informational brochures, and one-on-one discussions.
2. Data Privacy and Security
Ensuring all AI applications comply with data privacy regulations such as HIPAA in the US or GDPR in the EU is crucial. Patients need assurance that their personal health information is secure and will not be misused.
A recent report highlights the importance of data privacy and security in AI applications, noting that "generative AI systems in healthcare must be HIPAA compliant for data disclosures and secure to prevent breaches." Providing patients with control over their data, including the ability to consent to or opt out of AI-driven processes, helps build trust by ensuring they feel their privacy is respected.
3. Human Oversight
Maintaining a significant role for human clinicians in the AI process can enhance trust. Patients are more likely to trust AI-generated information if it is reviewed and validated by their healthcare providers.
Rep. Ted Lieu emphasized the need for human oversight in AI, stating, “Generative AI can absolutely improve health care delivery in a patient care setting. But it’s important that there’s a human being that double-checks that content generated by the AI.”
Recently, researchers at Mass General Brigham published a study showing the effectiveness of Gen AI tools in electronic medical records (EMRs). However, the report stipulated limitations of the tools that require human oversight.
4. Building Relationships
Strong relationships between patients and their healthcare providers are essential. Providers should take the time to explain how AI is being used to enhance care, ensuring that patients understand AI is a tool to support, not replace, their healthcare team.
Patrick Runnels, chief medical officer at University Hospitals, stated, “Patient-provider connectedness has to stay front and center. You can say, ‘We’re your care team — generative AI is helping us sort out your care on the back end, but you will always have a connection with your nurse, social worker or doctor.’”
Partnering with trusted community organizations to disseminate information about generative AI can help build broader acceptance and trust. These organizations can act as intermediaries, providing credible information to patients.
5. Addressing Ethical Concerns
Ensuring AI systems are free from biases and promoting equity in healthcare is critical. This involves using diverse datasets to train AI models and continuously monitoring for potential biases.
A December 2023 article from Nature discusses the importance of ethical principles in AI, proposing the “GREAT PLEA” ethical principles, which include Governability, Reliability, Equity, Accountability, Traceability, Privacy, Lawfulness, Empathy, and Autonomy.
Developing and adhering to ethical guidelines for AI use in healthcare can help build trust, ensuring principles such as safety, reliability, and fairness in AI development and deployment. Organizations such as the Coalition for Health AI (CHAI®) and the Responsible AI Institute (RAII) are a few growing organizations providing guidelines and benchmarks for ethical and responsible AI use.
6. Continuous Improvement and Feedback
Actively seeking and incorporating patient feedback on AI applications can help improve the technology and build trust.
Google’s Gemini model includes a comprehensive feedback management system where users can provide feedback on AI performance. This system helps improve AI quality and ensures that user concerns are addressed. Regularly auditing AI systems to ensure they function correctly and safely can help maintain trust, including monitoring for any inaccuracies or issues that may arise and addressing them promptly.
Moving Forward with Trust at the Center
The path to successfully integrating generative AI in healthcare lies in establishing and sustaining consumer trust. By addressing privacy concerns, engaging clinicians, being transparent, and collaborating with community partners, healthcare organizations can foster trust and increase the adoption of gen AI.
This trust will be instrumental in transforming gen AI from a promising tool into a trusted ally in achieving better health outcomes and more affordable healthcare.
The future of gen AI in healthcare is promising, but its success hinges on consumer trust. By committing to transparency, education, and collaboration, healthcare organizations can unlock the full potential of this transformative technology.

title: Council Post: AI For Agribusinesses: Unlocking Its Value In Operational Excellence
text:
Shashi Raghunandan, CEO of Oaken, is a hobby painter and a full-time husband and dog lover. He also sits on the board of MIFOS.
Much has been written about the application of AI in agriculture. The excitement is based on the convergence of large data generation at the farm level, a rise in computing power and improvements in technology that can aid in the need to produce significantly more food over the coming few decades.
AI technologies like image recognition are already deployed at scale in industries like food processing. The recent Forbes article by Ganes Kesari also highlights the applications of AI at the field level, from weed management to soil health. These are tremendous applications for AI with long-term benefits to the ecosystem, especially in the light of labor challenges.
Large enterprises with deep pockets have stepped up the application of AI in their products and equipment. John Deere, the pioneer of auto-driving and image recognition in agriculture states that their goal is to bring autonomy to all stages of crop production.
To tap into the opportunities that present themselves, image recognition, tagging the right plants at high speeds and coupling that with the mechanics of a robot requires the marrying of various engineering disciplines that take time and investment. And to realize these opportunities requires an appetite for risk and patient capital. SMBs account for a large part of any industry, and a recent Wall Street Journal article highlights (paywall) the challenges that these companies and startups alike face in implementing AI. The agricultural supply chain is especially concentrated with SMBs and the question that is foremost for CIOs is where to invest their dollars and at the same time see some immediate returns.
Operational Excellence: The Opportunity
McKinsey has recently cited three areas that have the potential to deliver outsized returns for agribusinesses looking to implement AI. These are R&D, Sales and Marketing and Operational Excellence. For SMBs, operational excellence offers an area to validate the impact of AI in a meaningful way. Operational excellence includes all areas of procurement, back office and accounting–the unglamorous underbelly of any organization.
Tasks and workflows that connect any organization and that need to be done are often repetitive but still take up time, effort and investment. In fact, according to a recent survey by Deloitte and Docusign, organizations with poor workflows spend an average of 18% more time, accounting for nearly $2 trillion in global economic value being eroded. This is a significant amount of time and resources for any small business and more importantly, is an area where AI performs really well.
SMBs in the agricultural space are especially exposed to these inefficacies. The agricultural supply chain supports multiple small businesses, and each of them manages multiple documents, leases and contracts as part of their daily operations. The need for AI in procurement is the most obvious with the ability to respond to RFP documents, synthesize contract terms and identify sources of value leakage to generate new negotiation techniques.
Another area that can benefit from the application of AI is the ingestion and summation of historic contracts, for example, farmland leases. OCR technologies can help read legacy legal contracts and make them easily readable and searchable, reducing time spent on these tasks. For example, the same Deloitte and Docusign study found that 54% of the respondents copy data manually from contracts and 49% say that they spend too much time searching for executed agreements. Therefore, operational excellence and the back-office is probably where SMBs could see some immediate ROI.
Recommendations For SMBs Looking To Implement AI
Organize the data. When it comes to supporting deployment, leaders will need to make decisions about how they store and manage their data. Paper documents, which are the norm among the older generation of farms and agribusinesses, need to be given way to modern technology that can make this efficiency realizable. This will require allocating technology budgets to get the plumbing right.
Prioritize the right use cases. Any agribusiness will have a range of use cases that are driven by its long-term goals. These goals could be anything from higher yields to better relationships with strategic partners to growing the business to even succession planning. Prioritizing the right use cases that can deliver the right ROI, not just monetarily, but as it relates to long-term priorities Is really important.
Identify the right partners. Legacy software systems or outdated systems can’t deliver the benefits of AI. Missing are the underlying data structures and the digital interfaces required to deliver the ROI. Identifying the right partner who is committed to implementing AI and delivering ROI for your business is absolutely critical.
Conclusion
It is easy to get sucked into the impact of any innovation. From the internet to mobile, the short-term impact is often overstated and the long-term impact is underestimated. Agribusiness leaders have the unenviable task of keeping their organization current while delivering ROI in the short term. In thinking of the challenges that this duality poses, operational excellence provides a unique opportunity to unlock the benefits that AI can deliver. It stands apart from use cases in R&D and Sales as it avoids heavier investments and uncertain returns and with its ubiquity it allows leaders to implement AI in the day-to-day operations of the organization.
In doing so, steps need to be taken to secure organization data, prioritizing the right use cases and identifying the right technology partners. If done right, this can bring the organization along in the AI journey and allow for time to upskill the employees to use the technology to their benefit, rather than be replaced by it.

title: Council Post: Navigating AI: The Future Of Work
text:
Martin Taylor is the Deputy CEO and co-founder of Content Guru.
During periods of extreme technological advancement, fears of mass unemployment have often accompanied the ground-breaking innovations of the day. From the creation of early agricultural machinery to the emergence of computers (in a time when "computer" was some people’s job title), each new wave of transformational invention has sparked concerns about job displacement, and it is no different when we look at the growth of artificial intelligence (AI). It is at once estimated that up to one-third of all jobs could be at risk of automation in the next decade and also that AI could create millions more jobs than it displaces.
Societal adaptation—some of it forced—to technological shifts is not a new phenomenon. The advent of the steam engine in the early 19th century, the mass production of steel in the 1850s and the rise of the internet in the 1990s all prompted widespread fears of established roles disappearing. Yet, history has shown that although certain occupations did cease to exist, new and generally better ones emerged. Indeed, 44% of organizations expect AI to lead to some layoffs in 2024. However, the same study also reveals a broader perspective: 96% of hiring companies believe candidates will benefit from having AI skills. This dichotomy underscores a critical point: Although AI will likely replace certain roles, headlines predicting widespread aggregate job losses fail to account for the wider picture.
A Rise In AI Roles—With More To Come
AI is poised to create whole new sectors and job roles, many of which we cannot yet envisage. It seems obvious now to record how the internet gave birth to e-commerce and an array of new business and employment opportunities, but most of those were far from apparent when the "Information Superhighway" first emerged from its laboratories.
Looking further back, in 1856, when steel production first became industrialized, shipping and railroads were seen as the areas most likely to be transformed. Few could have envisaged how the new technology would later enable the creation of the skyscraper and the automobile. Similarly, the early roles in AI development are iterations of existing occupations: From testing and deploying AI products to designing AI-driven customer experiences, there's a wealth of AI-created employment opportunities already, even before future waves of possibilities reveal themselves.
New, AI-powered or AI-supported roles will require a blend of traditional workplace skills and new, AI-specific competencies. Occupations created by AI will make up a fraction of the new “jobs of the future” that will employ today’s children, 65% of whom will be working in a job that doesn’t exist yet, according to a 2016 World Economic Forum report. Businesses that invest in retraining and upskilling their workforce stand to benefit the most, turning potential disruption into opportunities for growth, innovation and competitive advantage.
AI For CX: The Customer Experience Of The Future, Today
Although there must be a focus on creating new roles with AI, it is important to look at the industries where AI will make the biggest early impact and then assess the skills that the workforce of the future in those sectors will likely need.
The sector most likely to benefit from early AI transformation is customer experience (CX), with many business leaders identifying customer support roles in contact centers as one of the first places to benefit from AI's productivity increases. Professor Erik Brynjolfsson, a senior fellow at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research and Stanford Institute for Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence, reported up to 35% performance improvements in contact centers, which increases per-head productivity without necessarily replacing workers.
Instead of reducing headcount, businesses will be able to redeploy employees to areas where their skills can drive greater customer satisfaction and loyalty, such as becoming multiskilled service agents who work across a variety of communication channels. These AI-assisted agents benefit from a reduction in repetitive tasks such as collecting information around a customer query or searching for associated knowledge articles, the bulk of which can be automated to save time and improve job satisfaction. Suddenly, the skills required by an agent shift from administrative competence to becoming focused on building relationships with customers and delivering empathy, the “human touch” that customers increasingly demand.
Giving AI A Chance
Although the rise of AI does pose profound challenges to the future of the job market, it also offers unprecedented opportunities for growth and innovation. By learning from past workforce changes that resulted from technological shifts and proactively preparing for the future of AI, especially in CX, we as a society can navigate AI’s influence on the job market to the best effect. AI has the potential to transform whole industries, create new roles and enhance productivity, ensuring that the workforce of tomorrow is not only employed but also empowered by technology’s advancements.
